a: the Wilderness of Sin
p: Sin is a place name. Its location, like most stops on the route, is unknown.
b: The name has nothing to do with the English word "sin." It may be linked to the name Sinai, or to Sin, the moon god of Mesopotamia; no one knows. Travelers since the Middle Ages have placed it on the coastal plain of southwest Sinai (el-Markha) or the inland plain of Debbet er-Ramleh, but these guesses depend on the traditional location of Mount Sinai in the south of the peninsula (see 19:2). The date matters more to the story: the fifteenth of the second month is exactly one month after the night Israel left Egypt (12:6, 31). The food brought out of Egypt has run out.

a: complained
p: The Hebrew verb lun, "murmur, grumble," runs through the wilderness stories like a refrain.
b: The verb lun (the KJV's "murmur") appears in Exodus only in these chapters (15:24; 16:2, 7, 8; 17:3) and returns in Numbers 14, 16 and 17. It is a sullen, repeated complaining, often behind someone's back. The written text and the reading tradition differ slightly in spelling here (the Ketiv and Qere), with no change of sense. The New Testament uses these stories as warnings: "do not complain, the way some of them complained" (1 Corinthians 10:10), and Paul says these things were "written down as a warning for us" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Moses' answer in 16:8 is the key: complaints against God's leaders are complaints against God.
orig: וַיִּלּוֹנוּ (vayyillonu), "and they grumbled"

a: There we sat beside the pots of meat
p: Slaves in Egypt did not feast on meat. The people's memory has grown rosy in one month.
b: Egyptian work crews were paid mostly in bread and beer, with onions, beans, fish and now and then meat; records from the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina list such rations. The complaint is not an accurate memory but the kind of nostalgia hunger produces. Numbers 11:4–6 repeats it with a fuller menu: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic. The Bible often shows the danger of looking back to slavery as safety (Numbers 14:3–4; compare Lot's wife in Genesis 19:26). The phrase "die by the LORD's hand" is bitter: they would rather have died in the plagues than in the desert.

a: I am about to make bread fall like rain from the sky for you
p: Psalms, Nehemiah and John all retell this verse. Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven.
b: The verb is "rain down" (mamtir), the word used for the hail on Egypt (9:18) and the fire on Sodom (Genesis 19:24), here turned into a gift. Psalm 78:24–25 calls manna "the grain of heaven" and "the bread of the mighty ones," which the Septuagint and later Jews read as "the bread of angels" (also Wisdom 16:20). Nehemiah 9:15 recalls it in a prayer of confession. In John 6:31–35 the crowd quotes it to Jesus, and he answers that Moses did not give the true bread from heaven: "I am the bread of life." Christians have read the manna ever since as a picture of Christ and of the Lord's Supper.
r: Psalm 78:23–25; Psalm 105:40; Nehemiah 9:15, 20; Wisdom 16:20–21; John 6:31–51; 1 Corinthians 10:3

a: This is how I will test them: will they live by my law or not?
p: The manna is a daily test of trust. The word for "teaching" is torah, later the name of the whole Law.
b: God "tests" (nasah) Israel by making them depend on him one day at a time: they cannot store it, and they must stop on the seventh day. Deuteronomy 8:2–3 explains the lesson: God let them hunger and fed them manna "to teach you that a person does not live on bread alone, but on everything that comes from the LORD's mouth," words Jesus quotes when he is tested in the wilderness (Matthew 4:4). The word torah means "teaching" or "instruction." Here it means God's rules for the manna, but the same word becomes the name of the five books of Moses. This site renders it "teaching" so that its basic sense shows.
orig: בְּתוֹרָתִי (betorati), "in my teaching"

a: you will see the LORD's glory
p: The Hebrew kavod comes from a root meaning "heavy." God's glory is his presence made visible.
b: The word kavod comes from kaved, "to be heavy," the same root as "honor" your father (20:12). A person's "weight" is his importance. When the Bible speaks of "the glory of the LORD," it usually means something people can see: here a brightness in the cloud (16:10), later a devouring fire on the summit (24:17), and finally the glory filling the tabernacle (40:34–35). Isaiah hears the seraphim say the whole earth is full of it (Isaiah 6:3). John 1:14 picks up the image: the Word "pitched his tent among us, and we saw his glory."
orig: כְּבוֹד יְהוָה (kevod YHWH), "the glory of the LORD"

a: Between the two evenings
p: A Hebrew time phrase that most translations turn into "at twilight." Its exact meaning was debated.
b: The same phrase sets the time for killing the Passover lamb (12:6) and for the daily evening offering (29:39). What are the "two evenings"? The Pharisees and the later rabbis said the first evening begins when the sun starts to go down after noon and the second at sunset, so the Passover lambs were slaughtered in the afternoon (Josephus says from the ninth to the eleventh hour, about 3 to 5 p.m.). The Samaritans and the medieval Karaites took it as the time between sunset and full dark. Ibn Ezra held the Karaite-like view. The Plain English keeps the literal phrase; the gloss gives the common sense.
orig: בֵּין הָעַרְבַּיִם (bein ha'arbayim), "between the two evenings"

a: the quail came up and covered the camp
p: Migrating quail cross Sinai each spring and fall and drop to the ground worn out.
b: The common quail (Coturnix coturnix) migrates between Europe and Africa across the Sinai peninsula. In spring and autumn huge flocks come down exhausted on the Mediterranean coast, and Egyptians and Bedouin netted them there in large numbers into the twentieth century. The second month (about April or May) fits the spring migration. Exodus mentions the quail only briefly. Numbers 11:31–34 tells a second, darker quail story, when the birds came in heaps and a plague struck those who gorged on them, and Psalm 78:26–31 joins the two. Those who read the story as plain history point to this natural fit; others see a well-known desert event woven into the tradition.

a: something thin and flaky, thin like frost on the ground
p: Since 1927 many have linked manna to a sweet substance made by insects on tamarisk trees in Sinai.
b: In the Sinai, scale insects feeding on tamarisk trees give off a sweet liquid that dries into small sticky drops. Bedouin still call it mann. It forms overnight, must be gathered early before ants take it, and melts as the day warms, much as 16:21 says. F. S. Bodenheimer described it in 1947. But it appears only in early summer, in small amounts (a few hundred kilograms a year across the whole peninsula), and it does not double on Fridays or stop on Saturdays. Traditional readers see manna as a miracle that a natural food only resembles. Many scholars think the memory of this desert food was enlarged into the story of a nation fed for forty years.

a: What is it?
p: The name "manna" comes from the people's question. Man is an old word for "what."
b: The people say man hu. The usual Hebrew for "what" is mah, but man is known in Aramaic and in other Semitic languages, so the question "What is it?" sounds like a name: "It is man." Verse 31 makes the pun explicit: "The house of Israel gave it the name manna." The Greek Septuagint translates the question ("What is this?") and uses manna as the name. Rashi explains man as a portion of food, but most readers since antiquity hear the question; the Vulgate keeps manhu and explains it as "what is this?"
orig: מָן הוּא (man hu), "what is it?"

a: the one who gathered much had nothing left over
p: Paul quotes this verse to urge rich churches to share with poor ones.
b: In 2 Corinthians 8:13–15 Paul is raising money for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He wants "equality": the plenty of one church should meet the need of another. Then he quotes this verse: the one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little. The rabbis read the verse as a miracle: whatever each person gathered, at home it measured exactly an omer a head (Mekhilta; Rashi). Others read it as sharing in the camp. Either way the manna becomes a picture of an economy in which no one hoards and no one goes hungry.

a: It crawled with worms and smelled foul
p: Manna kept overnight spoiled. The lesson of trusting God one day at a time echoes in the Lord's Prayer.
b: Hoarded manna rots, but the double portion kept for the Sabbath does not (16:24). The point is not food storage but trust. Many Christian readers hear the manna behind the Lord's Prayer: "Give us today our bread for the day" (Matthew 6:11; the rare Greek word epiousios may mean "for today," "for tomorrow" or "needed"), and behind Jesus' words, "So do not fret over tomorrow" (Matthew 6:34). The rabbis drew the same lesson: "Whoever has something to eat today and says, 'What will I eat tomorrow?' is one of little faith" (a saying in the Mekhilta on this chapter, and in Sotah 48b).

a: double bread
t: Two loaves on the Sabbath table
p: The Jewish custom of two loaves of challah on the Sabbath comes from the double manna of this verse.
b: The Hebrew says they gathered lechem mishneh, "double bread." The Talmud teaches that on the Sabbath one should break bread over two loaves, in memory of this double portion (Shabbat 117b). That is why Jewish families set two loaves of challah on the table on Friday night. They are often covered with a cloth, which the tradition explains as the dew that lay above and below the manna (16:13–14). The leaders' report to Moses shows that this was something new: the rule of 16:5 had not yet been explained to the people.
orig: לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה (lechem mishneh), "double bread"

a: a holy Sabbath for the LORD
p: The word Sabbath appears here for the first time, before the Ten Commandments are given.
b: The noun shabbat comes from the verb shavat, "to stop, to cease." Genesis 2:2–3 used the verb for God's rest after creation but not the noun; this is the first time the Bible names "a Sabbath." The day is introduced as a gift (16:29) before it becomes a command (20:8). Jewish tradition says Israel first received some Sabbath laws at Marah (15:25; Sanhedrin 56b). Christians who see the Sabbath as built into creation point to Genesis 2; those who see it as a sign given to Israel point to this chapter and to 31:13–17, where it is called a sign between God and Israel. The word shabbaton ("a rest day") is a stronger form of the same word.
orig: שַׁבָּתוֹן שַׁבַּת־קֹדֶשׁ (shabbaton shabbat-qodesh), "a rest day, a holy Sabbath"

a: No one is to go out from where he is
p: The rabbis read this verse as a limit on how far one may walk on the Sabbath: 2,000 cubits.
b: Taken literally, "each of you stay put in your own spot" could mean not leaving the house at all, and some ancient groups read it strictly (the Damascus Document from Qumran limits Sabbath walking to 1,000 cubits outside a town, and 2,000 for pasturing animals). The rabbis read "place" as one's town and its surroundings, setting a limit (techum) of 2,000 cubits, about a kilometer, beyond the town (Eruvin 51a, linking it to Numbers 35:5). Acts 1:12 says the Mount of Olives is "a Sabbath day's journey" from Jerusalem, which shows the custom was known in Jesus' time.
orig: אַל־יֵצֵא אִישׁ מִמְּקֹמוֹ (al-yetse ish mimmeqomo), "let no one go out from his place"

a: It was like coriander seed, but white
p: Coriander seeds are small and round. Numbers adds that manna looked like bdellium, a pale resin.
b: Coriander seeds are small, ridged and round, usually tan rather than white, so the comparison is to size and shape. Numbers 11:7–8 adds that manna looked like bedolach, probably bdellium, a pale yellowish resin, and that people ground it, boiled it and made cakes that tasted like something made with olive oil. Here it tastes like a wafer with honey. Jewish legend solved the difference by saying manna tasted like whatever the eater wished (Yoma 75a; Wisdom 16:20–21 says it "suited every taste"). The Greek Septuagint describes it as "white like coriander seed."

a: to be kept safe for the generations after you
p: The jar of manna was kept with the ark. Hebrews puts it inside; later Jews said it was hidden away.
b: Hebrews 9:4 lists "a golden jar holding the manna" inside the ark of the covenant (the Septuagint here calls it a "golden" jar), while 1 Kings 8:9 says that by Solomon's day the ark held only the two tablets. Jewish tradition says Jeremiah showed the jar to his generation, saying in effect, "See what your ancestors lived on" (Mekhilta; Rashi, citing Jeremiah 2:31), and that King Josiah later hid it with the ark (Yoma 52b). Some Jewish texts expected the store of manna to come down again in the age of the Messiah (2 Baruch 29:8). Revelation 2:17 promises the faithful "the hidden manna."

a: he set it down before the testimony
t: The testimony that has not yet been given
p: "The testimony" means the stone tablets in the ark, which do not exist yet in the story.
b: The edut, "testimony" or "witness," is the name Exodus gives the tablets of the covenant, which are later placed in the ark (25:16; 31:18). At this point in the story Israel has not reached Sinai, and there is no ark and no tent. Traditional commentators explain that the command was given now but carried out later, once the tabernacle was built (Rashi; Ibn Ezra). Critical scholars see the verse as written from the point of view of a later time, when the tabernacle and its furniture were well known. Both agree that the narrator is looking ahead.
orig: לִפְנֵי הָעֵדֻת (lifnei ha'edut), "before the testimony"

a: For forty years the Israelites ate the manna
t: A verse written after the journey
p: This verse looks back over all forty years, so it was written at the end of the journey or later.
b: The verse describes the whole wilderness period as finished, and Joshua 5:12 records that the manna stopped the day after Israel ate the produce of Canaan at Gilgal. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers say Moses wrote it near the end of his life, on the plains of Moab at the border of Canaan, which fits the wording "until they arrived at the edge of the land". Some say Joshua or a later prophet added it. Critical scholars take verses like this, along with 16:36's explanation of an old measure, as signs that the book reached its present form long after the events. See the topic on the sources of the Pentateuch.

a: The omer is a tenth of an ephah.
p: An omer was roughly two quarts (about two liters) of grain. The note explains a measure readers had forgotten.
b: Scholars estimate the ephah at roughly 22 liters (about five or six US gallons, dry measure), though estimates range from about 10 to about 40 liters, so an omer was about two liters, a little over two quarts: enough flour for one person's bread for a day. The word omer as a measure appears only in this chapter; elsewhere it means a sheaf of grain (Leviticus 23:10–15, the source of the Jewish "counting of the Omer" between Passover and Shavuot). An editor's note like this assumes readers who no longer knew the unit, which most scholars take as a sign of a later hand.
orig: וְהָעֹמֶר עֲשִׂרִית הָאֵיפָה (veha'omer asirit ha'efah), "the omer is a tenth of the ephah"

a: camped at Rephidim
p: Rephidim's location is unknown. Tradition puts it in the Wadi Feiran, the largest oasis of south Sinai.
b: Numbers 33:12–14 lists two more stops, Dophkah and Alush, between the Wilderness of Sin and Rephidim. Since the Byzantine period, Christian pilgrims placed Rephidim in the Wadi Feiran, a long palm oasis on the way to the traditional Mount Sinai (Jebel Musa). The irony that an oasis would have "no water" did not trouble them, since the story is about a miracle. The location depends on where Mount Sinai was, which is not known (see 19:2). "Stage by stage" translates a word for the stages of a caravan's journey, the same word that heads the list of stops in Numbers 33.

a: What makes you test the LORD?
p: Deuteronomy turns this scene into a commandment, and Jesus quotes it when he is tempted.
b: To "test" God (nasah) is to demand that he prove himself on our terms. God may test his people (16:4; 20:20; Genesis 22:1), but the reverse is forbidden. Deuteronomy 6:16 makes the place a warning: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah." When the devil tells Jesus to throw himself from the temple and make God catch him, Jesus answers with that verse (Matthew 4:7; Luke 4:12). Psalm 95:7–11, quoted at length in Hebrews 3:7–4:11, also recalls Massah and Meribah as a day of hardened hearts.
r: Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 33:8; Psalm 95:7–11; Psalm 78:18–20; Matthew 4:7; Hebrews 3:7–11; 1 Corinthians 10:9

a: To make me and my children and my herds die of thirst?
p: The Hebrew has the people speak as one person: "me, my children, my herds."
b: Verse 3 shifts to the singular: "to kill me and my sons and my livestock." Most English versions smooth this into "us" and "our." The Hebrew often treats "the people" (ha'am) as a single person, and here the effect is vivid: the whole crowd speaks with one bitter voice, like one man watching his family die. The same grammar returns in a better moment at 19:2, where "Israel camped" is singular, and the rabbis drew a lesson from it there.
orig: אֹתִי (oti), "me"

a: on the rock at Horeb
p: Horeb is another name for the mountain of God. Here Israel is near it before reaching Sinai (19:1).
b: Exodus and Deuteronomy use two names for the mountain of revelation: Sinai (most of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers) and Horeb (3:1; 33:6; Deuteronomy; 1 Kings 19:8). Horeb may mean "dry place." Most readers take the two as one mountain, or Horeb as the wider region and Sinai as its peak. Here the puzzle is that Israel is at Horeb before it arrives at Sinai in 19:1. Traditional readers solve it by geography: Rephidim lay near the mountain range. Critical scholars connect the names with different sources: Horeb in the E source and Deuteronomy, Sinai in J and P.
orig: בְּחֹרֵב (beChorev), "at Horeb"

a: You will hit the rock, and water will flow out of it
p: Paul says "the rock was Christ." Jewish legend said the well followed Israel through the desert.
b: Water from the rock is recalled in Psalm 78:15–16; Psalm 105:41; Psalm 114:8 and Isaiah 48:21. Numbers 20:2–13 tells a second story at a place also called Meribah, where Moses strikes the rock twice instead of speaking to it and is barred from entering the land. Jewish tradition joined the stories into a traveling well, "Miriam's well," that rolled after Israel for forty years (Tosefta Sukkah 3:11; Pseudo-Philo, Biblical Antiquities 10:7). Paul seems to know such a tradition when he writes that Israel "drank from the spiritual rock that went with them, and the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Christians have also linked the struck rock to the pierced side of Jesus (John 19:34; compare John 7:37–39).
r: Numbers 20:2–13; Psalm 78:15–16; Psalm 105:41; Isaiah 48:21; 1 Corinthians 10:1–4; John 7:37–39; John 19:34

a: Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?
p: The quarrel about water is really a question about whether God is present.
b: The story ends with the question behind the complaint. Ramban noted that the people were not asking whether God exists but whether he is with them to provide, the same question that the tabernacle will answer (25:8; 29:45–46). The names fix the failure in memory: Massah means "Testing" and Meribah "Quarrel." Christian readers have heard an answer in the name Immanuel, "God with us" (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23), and in Jesus' last words "I myself am with you every day, until the completion of the age" (Matthew 28:20).

a: they put the LORD on trial
p: Judith retells Massah: a town without water sets God a deadline, and Judith calls it putting God to the test.
b: Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, builds a scene on this story. The Assyrians cut off the water of the town of Bethulia, and the thirsty people turn on their leaders, as Israel turned on Moses. The town's ruler, Uzziah, answers, "Take courage, brothers! Let us endure five more days" (Judith 7:30). If God has not helped by then, he will surrender. Judith sees the sin of Massah in this deadline. She asks the rulers, "Now who are you, to put God to the test today, and to stand in God's place among human beings?" (Judith 8:12). For her, trust means waiting on God without setting terms.

a: Then Amalek came and went to war against Israel
p: A nomad people of the Negev and Sinai, said to descend from Esau's grandson Amalek.
b: Genesis 36:12 traces Amalek to a grandson of Esau, so this is a war between relatives. The Amalekites appear in the Bible as raiders of the Negev and northern Sinai (Numbers 13:29; 1 Samuel 15:7; 1 Samuel 27:8; 1 Samuel 30:1). No inscription outside the Bible names them, which is not surprising for a tent-dwelling people. Deuteronomy 25:17–18 adds a detail Exodus leaves out: they struck from behind at the weak and weary stragglers. That cowardice is what makes Amalek, in later Jewish thought, the symbol of senseless cruelty.

a: Moses said to Joshua
p: Joshua enters the story without introduction. His name is the Hebrew original of the name Jesus.
b: Joshua is not introduced: we learn only later that he is the son of Nun, from Ephraim, and Moses' assistant (24:13; 33:11; Numbers 13:8, 16). Numbers 13:16 says Moses changed his name from Hoshea, "salvation," to Yehoshua, "the LORD saves." The Greek form of the name is Iēsous, the same name as Jesus, so Hebrews 4:8 can say "if Joshua had given them rest..." with a play on the name. Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr saw a deliberate pattern: Joshua ("Jesus") wins the battle while Moses' arms are stretched out (Justin, Dialogue 90 and 111).

a: As often as Moses raised his hand
t: Did Moses' hands win the battle?
p: The Mishnah says the hands turned Israel's hearts upward. Early Christians saw the shape of the cross.
b: The Mishnah asks the obvious question: "Did the hands of Moses make war or break war?" Its answer: when Israel looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven, they won; when they did not, they fell (Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Many Christian readers see raised hands as prayer (1 Timothy 2:8). The Epistle of Barnabas (Barnabas 12:2) and Justin Martyr (Dialogue 90) saw more: Moses with arms stretched out to both sides pictures the cross, by which the enemy is defeated. Some modern scholars think the staff of God (17:9) was held high as a battle standard, which would link this scene with the altar name in 17:15.

a: his hands stayed firm
p: The word for "firm" is emunah, the Hebrew word usually translated "faithfulness" or "faith."
b: The Hebrew says Moses' hands "were emunah," steadiness, until sundown. This is the first use in the Bible of the noun emunah, from the root aman, "to be firm, reliable" (the root of "amen"). Elsewhere emunah means faithfulness, as in Habakkuk 2:4, "the righteous will live by his faithfulness," quoted by Paul (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Targum Onqelos turned the image into prayer: his hands were "spread out in prayer." The picture is of leadership upheld by others: Aaron and Hur literally hold up Moses' hands.
orig: אֱמוּנָה (emunah), "steadiness, faithfulness"

a: Write this down in the scroll as a reminder
p: This is the first time God tells Moses to write. Tradition sees the start of the Torah's writing here.
b: Moses is told to write "in the scroll" (ba-sefer), with the definite article, as if a known record already exists. Later Moses writes "all the LORD's words" (24:4), the itinerary of the journey (Numbers 33:2) and the Torah itself (Deuteronomy 31:9, 24). Jewish and Christian tradition took these verses as evidence that Moses wrote the Pentateuch. Critical scholars note that the texts say Moses wrote specific records, not the five books as we have them; some think "the scroll" refers to an old collection like "the Book of the Wars of the LORD" (Numbers 21:14).
orig: כְּתֹב זֹאת זִכָּרוֹן בַּסֵּפֶר (ketov zot zikkaron basefer), "write this as a reminder in the scroll"

a: I will wipe out, yes, wipe out the memory of Amalek
p: Jews read Deuteronomy's "Remember Amalek" each year before Purim. The command troubles many readers.
b: Deuteronomy 25:17–19 turns this oath into a duty: "Remember what Amalek did to you... wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky. Do not forget." On the Sabbath before Purim, called Shabbat Zakhor, synagogues read that passage, because Haman in the book of Esther is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), a descendant of the Amalekite king Agag (1 Samuel 15). At the Purim reading, people drown out Haman's name with noise. Many Jewish and Christian readers are troubled by a command to wipe out a people. Later rabbis held that no people today can be identified as Amalek, since the Assyrian king Sennacherib long ago "mixed up the nations" (a principle found in Mishnah Yadayim 4:4), and many teachers read Amalek as the cruelty that preys on the weak, which each generation must fight in itself.
orig: מָחֹה אֶמְחֶה (macho emcheh), "I will surely wipe out"

a: The LORD Is My Flag
p: Nes means a pole or flag raised as a signal. Isaiah uses it for the Messiah, a "signal for the peoples."
b: The altar is named YHWH nissi. A nes is a pole or standard raised on a height as a rallying point for troops (Isaiah 5:26; Isaiah 13:2). The bronze serpent was put on a nes (Numbers 21:8–9), and Isaiah 11:10–12 says the root of Jesse will stand as a nes for the peoples. The KJV keeps the name as "Jehovahnissi," with "banner" in the margin, and most modern versions say "banner"; the Plain English says "flag" to keep the military picture plain. Christian readers link the raised standard to Jesus "lifted up" like the serpent (John 3:14; John 12:32). The name may also echo the raised hands and staff of 17:9–12.
orig: יְהוָה נִסִּי (YHWH nissi), "the LORD is my standard"
r: Numbers 21:8–9; Isaiah 11:10–12; Isaiah 49:22; Isaiah 62:10; John 3:14; John 12:32

a: A hand on the throne of the LORD!
t: A hard line: "a hand on the throne of Yah"
p: The Hebrew is obscure. It may be an oath, an accusation against Amalek, or a misread word for "flag."
b: The Hebrew reads ki yad al kes Yah, using a short form of God's name (Yah) and a word for "throne" (kes) found nowhere else. Three readings are common: (1) an oath with a hand raised to God's throne, "the LORD has sworn" (Rashi, Targum Onqelos); (2) an accusation: Amalek raised its hand against the LORD's throne (NIV, BSB); (3) a copying slip: change one letter and kes becomes nes, "flag," giving "a hand on the LORD's flag," which fits 17:15 (many critical scholars). (4) The Septuagint has "with a hidden hand," taking kes from kasah, "cover." Rashi adds a famous comment: God's name (Yah, not YHWH) and throne (kes, not kisse) are both shortened, because neither will be complete until Amalek's memory is wiped out.
orig: כִּי־יָד עַל־כֵּס יָהּ (ki-yad al-kes Yah), "for a hand on the throne of Yah"

a: Jethro, Midian's priest and father-in-law to Moses
p: Moses' father-in-law has three names in the Bible. The Midianites lived east of the Gulf of Aqaba.
b: He is Reuel in 2:18, Jethro in 3:1 and here, and Numbers 10:29 speaks of "Hobab son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law," while Judges 4:11 calls Hobab himself Moses' father-in-law. Some think Jethro is a title ("his excellency") and Reuel a clan name; the rabbis said he had seven names (Mekhilta). Midian was a region of northwest Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba; Midianite painted pottery of about the 1200s BC, first known from Qurayyah there, has also been found at the Egyptian copper mines of Timna in the Arabah. Judges 1:16 calls his descendants Kenites, who settled with Judah.

a: Moses had sent his wife Zipporah back
p: Exodus never tells us when Moses sent Zipporah home. The word may even suggest a divorce.
b: In 4:20 Moses set out for Egypt with his wife and sons, and in 4:24–26 Zipporah saved his life on the way. Now we learn she is back with her father. The word shilluchim, "sending away," is used for a dowry or parting gift (1 Kings 9:16) and is related to the verb for divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1). The Mekhilta gives two views: Moses divorced her, or he only sent her home. A famous midrash says Aaron met them on the road and said, "We are grieving for those already in Egypt, and you bring more?" so Moses sent them back (Mekhilta; Rashi on 4:20 and 18:2). Numbers 12:1 later mentions a Cushite wife.
orig: אַחַר שִׁלּוּחֶיהָ (achar shilluchehah), "after her sending away"

a: One son's name was Gershom
p: Gershom sounds like "a foreigner there." Eliezer means "My God is help."
b: Gershom's name was explained already in 2:22; it sounds like ger sham, "a foreigner there." Eliezer, named only here, means "my God is help," and the explanation looks back to Moses' escape from Pharaoh, who wanted to kill him (2:15). The order matters: the first son remembers exile, the second rescue. Neither son plays any later role. 1 Chronicles 23:14–17 counts them among the Levites, and Judges 18:30 says a grandson of Gershom became priest at the idol shrine of Dan; the Hebrew there has a raised letter n that turns "Moses" into "Manasseh," probably to spare Moses' name.
orig: גֵּרְשֹׁם (Gershom); אֱלִיעֶזֶר (Eliezer)

a: to where Moses was camping by the mountain of God
p: Israel reaches Sinai only in 19:1, yet Jethro finds them at the mountain of God. Did he come later?
b: The rabbis argued whether Jethro came before the Ten Commandments or after (Zevachim 116a). Ibn Ezra held that he came after the law was given and that the story was placed here on purpose, to set the friendly Midianite beside the hostile Amalek (17:8–16). Ramban argued for the order as written. Several details support Ibn Ezra: Jethro offers sacrifices on an altar (18:12), Moses teaches "God's rules and his laws" (18:16), and Deuteronomy 1:9–18 places the appointing of judges after the stay at Horeb. Numbers 10:29–32 has Hobab leaving only when Israel departs from Sinai. Many modern scholars agree that the chapter is placed by theme, not by time.

a: bowed low, and kissed him
p: Bowing and kissing showed honor to an elder. Moses, the leader of a nation, honors his father-in-law.
b: Bowing to the ground and kissing were the standard greetings between relatives and before a superior (Genesis 29:13; Genesis 33:3–4; 2 Samuel 14:33). "Each asked how the other was doing" is literally "they asked each other about shalom," about peace or well-being, the Hebrew way of saying hello. The rabbis noticed that the verse does not say who kissed whom, and they read it as Moses honoring Jethro, the leader of Israel bowing to a foreign priest (Mekhilta). The scene is warm on purpose: it is the opposite of Amalek's ambush in the chapter before.

a: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods
p: Jewish tradition says Jethro became the first convert. Others hear praise from a priest of another god.
b: Jethro praises the LORD, blesses him (18:10) and offers sacrifice (18:12). The Mekhilta and later midrash tell that Jethro had tried every idol in the world before declaring the LORD greatest, and that he became a convert (ger). The Torah portion that contains the Ten Commandments (Exodus 18–20) is named Yitro after him, which Jewish teachers see as an honor given to an outsider whose advice shaped Israel's courts. Christian readers often place him with Melchizedek, Rahab, Ruth and Naaman as Gentiles who recognized Israel's God. Some modern scholars read his words differently: he says "greater than all the gods," which does not yet deny that other gods exist (compare 15:11).

a: took a whole burnt offering and sacrifices for God
p: Some scholars think the worship of YHWH came to Israel from Midian, by way of Jethro.
b: Jethro, a foreign priest, leads a sacrifice to Israel's God, and Aaron and the elders come to eat with him. Since the 1800s some scholars (Ghillany, Budde, later H. H. Rowley and Joseph Blenkinsopp) have suggested that Moses learned the worship of YHWH from the Midianites or Kenites. They point to this scene, to God's appearance to Moses in Midian (3:1), to old poems in which the LORD comes "from Seir," "from Teman" and "from Paran" in the south (Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4; Habakkuk 3:3), and to Egyptian lists from the 1300s BC that name "the land of the Shasu of Yhw," a nomad region south of Canaan. Others answer that the text presents Jethro learning about the LORD from Moses (18:8–11), not the reverse. The theory remains debated.

a: to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God
p: Aaron and the elders eat with Jethro "in front of God," but Moses is not mentioned.
b: "To eat bread" means to share a meal, often a meal that seals friendship or a covenant (Genesis 31:54). Here it follows a sacrifice, so it is a sacred meal "before God," that is, at an altar or a holy place. Moses' absence from the list puzzled readers. The Mekhilta answers that Moses stood and served them, as Abraham served his guests (Genesis 18:8). The scene looks ahead to 24:9–11, when Moses, Aaron and the elders eat and drink in God's presence on the mountain.

a: to seek God's answer
p: The people came to Moses for rulings from God, as later Israelites went to prophets and priests.
b: The verb darash, "seek, inquire," with God as object means asking God for a decision, often through a prophet or priest (1 Samuel 9:9; 1 Kings 22:8). Moses is both judge and prophet: cases come to him, and he makes known God's rulings (18:16; Numbers 15:32–36 and Numbers 27:1–11 show him bringing hard cases to God). Later Jewish law placed the hardest cases before the high court at the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 17:8–12). The word midrash, the rabbis' name for searching out the meaning of Scripture, comes from the same root.
orig: לִדְרֹשׁ אֱלֹהִים (lidrosh Elohim), "to seek God"

a: God's rules and his laws
p: Exodus uses several words for God's law. This site keeps one English word for each.
b: Three Hebrew words for law meet in these chapters. Chuqqim, from a root meaning "to carve," are fixed rules; this site says "rules." Torot (singular torah) are instructions or teachings; this site says "law" (see 16:4), the sense the word has as the name of the five books. Mishpatim, from shaphat, "to judge," are rulings made by a judge, the case laws of 21:1; this site says "rulings." Commands are mitsvot. Later Jewish tradition sometimes contrasts chuqqim, laws without a stated reason, with mishpatim, laws that reason can grasp (Rashi on Leviticus 18:4).
orig: חֻקֵּי הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֶת־תּוֹרֹתָיו (chuqqei ha'Elohim ve'et-torotav)

a: men of worth, who fear God, men of truth who hate crooked profit
p: Jethro's four qualities for judges reappear in Deuteronomy and, in a new form, in the early church.
b: Jethro asks for ability (chayil, strength, worth), fear of God, truthfulness and hatred of betsa, gain made by cheating or bribes. Deuteronomy 1:13–17 retells the scene, asking for "wise, discerning and well-known" men and adding the charge to judge small and great alike. Deuteronomy 16:18–20 forbids bribes, for "a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise." When the apostles appoint seven men to oversee food for widows, they look for men filled with the Spirit and with wisdom (Acts 6:3). Maimonides lists seven qualities for a judge, drawing on this verse (Mishneh Torah, Laws of the Sanhedrin 2:7).
orig: אַנְשֵׁי־חַיִל יִרְאֵי אֱלֹהִים אַנְשֵׁי אֱמֶת שֹׂנְאֵי בָצַע (anshei-chayil yir'ei Elohim anshei emet son'ei vatsa)

a: captains of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens
p: The units sound military. The word for "thousand" can also mean a clan, which matters for Israel's numbers.
b: The ranks of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens match army units (Numbers 31:14; 1 Samuel 8:12; 2 Kings 1:9). Exodus 12:37 counts about 600,000 men on foot, which with families would mean two million people or more. The Hebrew elef, "thousand," can also mean a clan or a military unit (Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19). George Mendenhall (1958) and Colin Humphreys (1998) argued that the census numbers originally counted such units, giving a much smaller nation, perhaps 20,000 people. Traditional readers defend the large numbers as written; most critical scholars think the numbers are not historical, however one reads elef.
orig: שָׂרֵי אֲלָפִים (sarei alafim), "officers of thousands"

a: If you do this, and God commands you
p: Moses takes advice from a Midianite. Jewish and Christian teachers drew lessons about leadership and humility.
b: Jethro is careful: his plan holds only "if God so commands you." Moses accepts it at once (18:24). The rabbis praised both men: "Who is wise? The one who learns from everyone" (Avot 4:1). Christian teachers have used the chapter for church leadership: Moses' burden is too heavy for one person, as Numbers 11:14–17 says in Moses' own complaint, and God answers there by sharing his spirit with seventy elders. The image of carrying the load together (18:22) is close to Paul's "carry one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2). Some critical scholars think the story explains the origin of Israel's court system by tying it to Moses.

a: Jethro made his way back to his own land
p: Jethro goes home, but his family's story continues with the Kenites, Jael and the Rechabites.
b: In Numbers 10:29–32 Moses asks Hobab to stay and be Israel's "eyes" in the desert; the answer is not recorded, but Judges 1:16 says the Kenites, Moses' in-laws, went up with Judah. Jael, the heroine who kills Sisera, is the wife of Heber the Kenite (Judges 4:11, 17–22). Saul spares the Kenites because they showed kindness to Israel when it came up from Egypt (1 Samuel 15:6). 1 Chronicles 2:55 links the Rechabites, famous for their faithfulness in Jeremiah 35, to the Kenites. The friendly foreigner of this chapter thus has a long and honored line.
r: Numbers 10:29–32; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11, 17–22; 1 Samuel 15:6; 1 Chronicles 2:55; Jeremiah 35:1–19

a: on this same day
p: Jewish tradition counts from here to the sixth of Sivan, the day of Shavuot, as the day the Torah was given.
b: "On this same day" seems to point to the first day of the third month: the Hebrew chodesh means both "month" and "new moon" (Rashi). Counting the three days of 19:10–16, the rabbis dated the giving of the Ten Commandments to the sixth (or seventh) of the month Sivan (Shabbat 86b). That made the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, fifty days after Passover, into "the season of the giving of our Torah," a meaning the Bible itself never states. The chapter page for chapter 24 traces the feast from Jubilees to Pentecost.
orig: בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁי (bachodesh hashelishi), "in the third month" or "at the third new moon"

a: Israel camped there
p: The Hebrew verb is singular: "Israel camped." The rabbis heard a nation united for once.
b: The first verbs of 19:2 are plural ("they set out... they entered... they pitched camp"), but then the Hebrew switches to the singular: vayyichan, "and he camped," with Israel as one person. The Mekhilta and Rashi comment that at every other camp Israel quarreled, but here they camped "as one person with one heart." The grammar is normal Hebrew for a group noun, but the switch in one verse invited the lesson. Compare the united answer of 19:8 and 24:3, where the whole people answers "with a single voice."
orig: וַיִּחַן־שָׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל (vayyichan-sham Yisra'el), "and Israel camped there"

a: facing the mountain
p: No one knows. The main candidates are in southern Sinai, northern Sinai, the Negev and northwest Arabia.
b: Exodus never gives directions, and Jewish tradition never marked the spot. The best-known candidate, Jebel Musa ("Mount of Moses") in southern Sinai, has been honored by Christian monks since the 300s; the Monastery of St. Catherine was built at its foot under the emperor Justinian (about 550). Earlier Christian tradition sometimes pointed to nearby Jebel Serbal. Others place Sinai in northern Sinai (Jebel Sin Bishar, Jebel Helal), at Har Karkom in the Negev (Emmanuel Anati, who found many shrines there, though most date long before any likely exodus), or in Midian in northwest Arabia, since Moses met God in Midian (3:1) and Paul writes of "Mount Sinai in Arabia" (Galatians 4:25). Popular claims that Jebel al-Lawz in Saudi Arabia shows the burned summit and the altar are not accepted by archaeologists. See the chapter page.

a: I lifted you up on the wings of eagles
p: The great bird that carries its young is an image of God's care. The bird may be an eagle or a vulture.
b: The Hebrew nesher can mean the eagle or the griffon vulture, the largest bird of the region; Micah 1:16 speaks of the nesher's bald head, which fits the vulture. Deuteronomy 32:11 expands the picture: like a nesher stirring its nest and hovering over its young, God spread his wings and carried Israel. Rashi adds that other birds carry their young in their claws, but the eagle carries them on its wings, so that any arrow must pass through the parent first. Isaiah 40:31 promises that those who hope in the LORD will rise on wings like eagles, and in Revelation 12:14 the woman is given the wings of the great eagle to flee into the wilderness.
orig: עַל־כַּנְפֵי נְשָׁרִים (al-kanfei nesharim), "on wings of eagles"

a: my own private treasure
p: Segullah is the personal property a king keeps for himself, apart from the kingdom's wealth.
b: In 1 Chronicles 29:3 David gives his own segullah, his private gold and silver, to the temple, beyond what he had set aside from the kingdom (compare Ecclesiastes 2:8). The same idea appears in Akkadian as sikiltu, a word used both for private savings and, on a royal seal from Alalakh, for a king as the "treasured possession" of his god (Moshe Greenberg, 1951). The verse then adds "for the whole earth belongs to me": Israel is chosen not because God owns nothing else but because, owning everything, he sets this people apart. Deuteronomy 7:6 and Deuteronomy 14:2 repeat the phrase, Malachi 3:17 uses it for the faithful, and Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 2:9 apply it to the church.
orig: סְגֻלָּה (segullah), "treasured possession"
r: Deuteronomy 7:6; Deuteronomy 14:2; Deuteronomy 26:18; Psalm 135:4; Malachi 3:17; Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 2:9

a: if you really listen to my voice and keep my covenant
p: God reminds Israel what he has done before he gives terms. Readers debate how conditional the covenant is.
b: The order of 19:4–6 is the order of the whole Sinai covenant: first what God has done ("I lifted you up"), then what he asks ("if you listen"), then what he promises ("you will be my treasure"). In the 1950s George Mendenhall compared this pattern with Hittite vassal treaties, which open with a history of the great king's kindness before listing duties and blessings; Kenneth Kitchen argues the closest match is with treaties of the 1300s and 1200s BC, while others compare Assyrian treaties of the 600s. Jewish readers stress that the commandments are Israel's grateful answer to rescue. Christian readers ask how this "if" relates to God's promise to Abraham; Paul argues that the law, coming 430 years later, cannot cancel the promise (Galatians 3:17).
orig: אִם־שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ בְּקֹלִי וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת־בְּרִיתִי (im-shamoa tishme'u beqoli ushmartem et-beriti)

a: a kingdom of priests, a holy nation
p: Peter and Revelation apply these words to the church. Readers ask whom Israel's priesthood serves.
b: What does it mean for a whole nation to be priests? Some say Israel stands between God and the nations as priests stand between God and the people, teaching and blessing the world (compare Isaiah 61:6, "you will be called priests of the LORD"). Others read "a kingdom ruled by priests" or, with Rashi, "a kingdom of princes." The Greek Septuagint has basileion hierateuma, "a royal priesthood," the exact words of 1 Peter 2:9, which applies the verse to believers in Christ (also Revelation 1:6; Revelation 5:10). Martin Luther built his teaching of "the priesthood of all believers" largely on 1 Peter 2:9. Jewish readers note that Israel remains God's holy nation (Deuteronomy 7:6).
orig: מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים וְגוֹי קָדוֹשׁ (mamlekhet kohanim vegoi qadosh)
r: Isaiah 61:6; 1 Peter 2:5, 9; Revelation 1:6; Revelation 5:10; Revelation 20:6; Deuteronomy 7:6

a: Then Moses reported the people's words to the LORD.
p: Moses has already reported the people's answer in 19:8. The repetition puzzled ancient and modern readers.
b: Verse 8 already says that Moses carried the people's reply back to the LORD, and verse 9 says it again. Rashi, following the Mekhilta, explains that this was a second answer: the people said they wanted to hear directly from their King, not through a messenger, and so God promised to speak where they could hear (19:9; 20:22). Others take it as a summary that resumes the story after God's words. Critical scholars see one of several signs that chapter 19 joins more than one account; the movements of Moses up and down the mountain (19:3, 7, 8, 14, 20, 25) are hard to follow as a single sequence.

a: set them apart as holy
p: To be holy here means to be ready to meet God: washing clothes and keeping apart from sex.
b: Qiddesh, "make holy," here means preparing for an encounter: washing clothes (19:10, 14), keeping back from the mountain (19:12) and abstaining from sex (19:15; compare Leviticus 15:18 and 1 Samuel 21:4–5, where David's men are "kept from women" before eating holy bread). Holiness in the Bible is not first of all moral goodness but belonging to God and being fit for his presence. Jacob gave a similar order before going to Bethel: "Make yourselves clean and change your clothes" (Genesis 35:2). The three days of preparation became a pattern; many Christians link the "third day" here with the third day of the resurrection.
orig: וְקִדַּשְׁתָּם (veqiddashtam), "and make them holy"

a: Whoever touches the mountain must be put to death.
t: A mountain no one may touch
p: Holiness is dangerous. Hebrews quotes this warning to contrast Sinai with the heavenly Mount Zion.
b: The mountain becomes like the later sanctuary, with zones of holiness: the people below, the priests and elders partway (24:1–2), and Moses alone at the top, as only the high priest entered the holy of holies (Leviticus 16). Many scholars, Jewish and Christian, see Sinai as the model for the tabernacle that will carry its fire and cloud with Israel (40:34–38). The danger of touching holy things returns in the story of Uzzah (2 Samuel 6:6–7). Hebrews 12:18–21 recalls the order that even a beast touching the mountain was to be stoned, and then says: you have not come to that mountain, but to Mount Zion and the city of the living God (12:22–24).

a: When the ram's horn sounds a long blast
p: The word here, yovel, also names the Jubilee year. And who are "they" who may go up?
b: Two words for horn appear in this chapter: shofar (19:16, 19) and here yovel, "ram's horn." Yovel later names the fiftieth year, the Jubilee, announced with a horn (Leviticus 25:9–13), and the English word "jubilee" comes from it through Latin. The sentence is unclear about who may go up when it sounds: the people (Rashi says it marks the end of God's presence on the mountain, when the ban is lifted), or only those chosen (Moses, Aaron, the elders, 19:24; 24:1). Some read "they may come up to the mountain" as "approach," not "climb."
orig: בִּמְשֹׁךְ הַיֹּבֵל הֵמָּה יַעֲלוּ בָהָר (bimshokh hayyovel hemmah ya'alu vahar)

a: Do not come near a woman
p: Moses addresses the men. Some readers see women left out of the moment of revelation.
b: Moses turns God's command to "set them apart" into an order not to approach a woman, which assumes a male audience. Judith Plaskow's Standing Again at Sinai (1990) made this verse the starting point of a Jewish feminist theology: at the founding moment of the covenant, women seem to be outside the "you." Traditional readers answer that the women were present and included: the Mekhilta reads "the house of Jacob" in 19:3 as the women, addressed first and gently, and "the Israelites" as the men. Deuteronomy 29:10–11 names women and children among those entering the covenant. Some modern scholars read the verse as purity law addressed to husbands, not as exclusion.

a: there was thunder
p: The Hebrew for thunder is qolot, "voices." The scene is full of sounds before God speaks.
b: Qolot is the plural of qol, "voice, sound." The same word is the horn's "sound" (19:16, 19), God's answering "voice" (19:19) and the "thunder" the people "see" in 20:18. English has to choose; Hebrew lets thunder, trumpet and speech blur together. The rabbis taught that God's voice at Sinai divided into seventy voices, for the seventy nations (Shabbat 88b, on Psalm 68:12), and Philo said the voice became visible flame (On the Decalogue 46). Christian readers compare Pentecost, where a sound from heaven and tongues like fire came on the disciples (Acts 2:2–3).
orig: קֹלֹת (qolot), "voices, thunders"

a: a heavy cloud on the mountain
p: Thunder, lightning and quaking mountains were the language of storm gods. Israel's account is different.
b: Neighbors of Israel described their storm gods in the same terms: in the Ugaritic poems from about 1300 BC, Baal "gives forth his holy voice" and the earth shakes (the Baal Cycle). Psalm 29, Judges 5:4–5, Psalm 18:7–15 and Habakkuk 3 use the same imagery for Israel's God. Most scholars think Israel borrowed a shared poetic language to say that its God is the true lord of the storm. The differences are just as striking: at Sinai the storm is not a battle against chaos or death but the setting for words, and no form of God is seen (Deuteronomy 4:12: "you were seeing no form. There was nothing but a voice"; compare Deuteronomy 4:15).
r: Psalm 18:7–15; Psalm 29:3–9; Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:3–6; Deuteronomy 4:11–15; 1 Kings 19:11–12

a: They stood in place beneath the mountain
p: A Talmud teacher read "beneath the mountain" literally: God held Sinai over Israel like a tub.
b: The Hebrew betachtit hahar usually means "at the foot of the mountain," but it can mean "underneath." Rav Avdimi bar Hama read it that way: God turned the mountain over them like a barrel and said, "If you accept the Torah, good; if not, there will be your grave" (Shabbat 88a). Another rabbi objected that a covenant made under force could be disowned. Rava answered that Israel accepted it again freely in the days of Esther (Esther 9:27, "they took on themselves"). The story raises a real question: is a covenant with an almighty God ever simply free? It sits beside the eager "we will do" of 19:8 and 24:7.
orig: בְּתַחְתִּית הָהָר (betachtit hahar), "at the bottom of the mountain"

a: Mount Sinai smoked from top to bottom
p: Smoke, fire and quaking have suggested a volcano to some. The Sinai peninsula has no active volcanoes.
b: Some readers since the 1800s have read the smoke "like a furnace," the fire and the quaking as a volcanic eruption. Charles Beke (1873) and, more recently, Colin Humphreys (2003) used this to argue that Sinai lay in northwest Arabia, where there are volcanic fields that were active in historical times; the Sinai peninsula itself has none. Others answer that the language is the stock imagery of a storm theophany (see 19:16) and that the same words describe God's coming elsewhere (Psalm 104:32; Psalm 144:5). Traditional readers take the scene as a supernatural event beyond natural explanation.
r: Genesis 15:17; Genesis 19:28; Psalm 104:32; Psalm 144:5; Deuteronomy 4:11; Deuteronomy 5:23

a: God kept answering him with a voice
p: The phrase can mean God answered in thunder, or in words. Who heard the Ten Commandments, and how?
b: Beqol can mean "with a voice," "aloud" or "in thunder." The tenses describe repeated action: Moses would speak, and God would answer. Rashi says God gave Moses' voice the strength to be heard over the horn. Ibn Ezra and others think God answered Moses in audible words. The verse leads into a larger question: did all Israel hear the Ten Commandments from God, as 20:1 and Deuteronomy 5:4, 22 suggest, or did Moses relay them, as Deuteronomy 5:5 says ("I stood between the LORD and you")? The Talmud reports a view that the people heard only the first two directly (Makkot 24a), since those two speak of God as "I."
orig: וְהָאֱלֹהִים יַעֲנֶנּוּ בְקוֹל (veha'Elohim ya'anennu veqol)

a: The priests too
p: Aaron's sons are not made priests until Exodus 28–29 and Leviticus 8. Who are these priests?
b: Israel has no ordained priesthood yet. The rabbis said these "priests" were the firstborn sons, who served before the Levites replaced them (Zevachim 115b; Rashi; compare Numbers 3:12–13 and the "young men" who offer sacrifices in Exodus 24:5). Others think of family heads or of Jethro's kind of priest (18:12). Some critical scholars see a sign of a later writer, for whom priests were part of every scene at the sanctuary. The verse also shows how the mountain works like a temple: even those who draw near must be specially prepared.

a: or he will break out against them
p: The people must not "break through" (haras); if they do, God will "break out" (parats) against them.
b: Two verbs answer each other: if the people haras, tear down the boundary, the LORD will parats, burst out. Parats is the root of the name Perez, the twin who "broke out" first (Genesis 38:29), and of Perez-uzzah, the place where the LORD "burst out" against Uzzah for touching the ark (2 Samuel 6:8). God's holiness is not a fence that protects God; it protects the people from a presence they cannot survive unprepared.
orig: יֶהֶרְסוּ (yehersu), "they break through"; יִפְרָץ־ (yifrots), "he bursts out"

a: Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.
p: The Hebrew says Moses "said to them," but no words follow. The Ten Commandments begin instead.
b: The Hebrew vayyomer alehem normally introduces a quotation, but chapter 19 ends with nothing quoted, and 20:1 begins with God speaking. Traditional readers say Moses delivered the warnings just given (19:21–24), and that 20:1 follows naturally. Many critical scholars think the Ten Commandments (20:1–17) were inserted into an older story in which 19:25 led directly to 20:18, where the people react to the thunder; the effect is that Moses is still at the foot of the mountain when God speaks. The Plain English "spoke to them" smooths this slightly.
orig: וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם (vayyomer alehem), "and he said to them"

a: Then God spoke all these words
p: The Bible calls them "the ten words," not "commandments." Who heard them, and how, was debated.
b: Exodus 34:28 and Deuteronomy 4:13; Deuteronomy 10:4 call them aseret hadevarim, "the ten words" or "ten sayings"; the Greek dekalogos, "Decalogue," means the same. Only here in the Torah does God speak a law directly to the whole people. Deuteronomy says God spoke "face to face... out of the fire" (Deuteronomy 5:4) but also that Moses stood between (Deuteronomy 5:5). The Talmud reports that Israel heard only the first two words from God himself (Makkot 24a); a Hasidic saying, made famous by Gershom Scholem, claims they heard only the silent first letter, the aleph of anokhi, "I." Christian writers stressed that these words were written by God's own finger (31:18). Later tradition also said the law came through angels (Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek; Acts 7:38, 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2).
orig: וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֵת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה (vaydabber Elohim et kol-hadevarim ha'elleh)
r: 34:28; 31:18; Acts 7:38, 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2; Deuteronomy 4:12–13; Deuteronomy 5:4–5, 22; Deuteronomy 10:4

a: I am the LORD your God.
t: The first word: a statement, not a command
p: In Jewish counting this verse is the first of the Ten Words. Christians usually treat it as a preface.
b: The first "word" commands nothing; it states who is speaking and what he has done. In the Jewish tradition (the Mekhilta, the Talmud and the synagogue's division of the text) this verse is the first of the ten. Maimonides counted it as the first of the 613 commandments: the command to believe that God exists (Sefer HaMitzvot, positive command 1), while others, such as the medieval Halakhot Gedolot, did not count a belief as a commandment. Christian traditions treat the verse as the preface to the commands. Either way, grace comes first: God reminds Israel that he freed them before he tells them how to live as free people.
orig: אָנֹכִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ (anokhi YHWH Eloheikha), "I am the LORD your God"

a: I brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves.
p: Every "you" in the Ten Words is singular. Each Israelite is addressed as a single person.
b: Hebrew distinguishes "you" singular from "you" plural. Chapter 19 used the plural; the Ten Words switch to the singular: "your God," "I brought you." Philo of Alexandria asked why and answered that God wanted each listener to feel addressed personally, as if the whole law were spoken to him alone (On the Decalogue 36–39). The phrase "house of slaves" (beit avadim) pictures Egypt as one huge slave barracks. The same slave word, eved, returns in 20:10 and 21:2: the people freed from slavery must now make rules for the slaves in their own houses.
orig: מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים (mibbeit avadim), "from a house of slaves"

a: in my presence
p: The Hebrew al panai literally means "on my face." It can mean before me, besides me, or in defiance of me.
b: The phrase al panai can mean "in front of, in the presence of" (Genesis 11:28, literally), "besides, in addition to," or "to the face of," that is, against (as in Job 1:11, "to your face"). So the command may forbid worshiping other gods in God's sight (Rashi: anywhere, since God sees everywhere), or having any god besides him, or setting up a rival against him. Scholars debate whether the verse assumes other gods exist (some call this "monolatry": worship of one god among many) or simply forbids Israel to treat anything as a god. Later texts state plainly that there is no other god at all (Deuteronomy 4:35, 39; Isaiah 45:5–6).
orig: עַל־פָּנָי (al panai), "on my face"

a: You must not have any other gods in my presence.
p: Jews, Catholics and Lutherans, and most other Protestants and the Orthodox divide the same verses differently.
b: The text has more than ten imperatives, so traditions group them differently. Jewish: (1) 20:2; (2) 20:3–6, other gods and images together; then name, Sabbath, parents, murder, adultery, stealing, false witness, and (10) coveting. Catholic and Lutheran, following Augustine: (1) 20:3–6; (2) the name; (3) Sabbath; ... then two craving commands: Catholics, with Deuteronomy 5:21, (9) wife, (10) goods; Lutherans, with Exodus 20:17, (9) house, (10) wife and the rest. Reformed, Anglican and Orthodox, following Philo, Josephus and Origen: (1) other gods; (2) images; ... (10) all coveting. The Samaritans treat 20:2 as a preface, count 20:3–6 as one, and make the tenth a command to build an altar on Mount Gerizim (see the variant at 20:17). The chapter page compares the systems in a table.

a: You must not make yourself an idol
t: Images: Jewish, Christian and Muslim answers
p: Is this a ban on all images, on images of God, or on images made to worship?
b: Judaism has always forbidden any image of God and long avoided statues in worship, though ancient synagogues such as Dura-Europos (AD 240s) were painted with biblical scenes. Christians split over icons. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) ruled that icons may be venerated, honored with a kiss or a candle, but that worship belongs to God alone; the Eastern iconoclasts had argued the opposite. At the Reformation, Lutherans kept crucifixes and paintings, while Reformed churches removed them and counted this verse as a separate commandment (Calvin, Institutes 1.11). Islam's avoidance of images in mosques reflects a similar instinct. All agree that the core is: do not make what you can control and call it God.
orig: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה־לְךָ פֶסֶל (lo ta'aseh-lekha fesel), "do not make yourself a carved image"
r: 32:1–8; Deuteronomy 4:15–19; Deuteronomy 27:15; Isaiah 44:9–20; Acts 17:29; Romans 1:22–23; 1 John 5:21

a: or the form of anything up in the sky, or down on the earth, or in the waters below the land
t: Did Israel make images of God?
p: Archaeology shows that Israel's official worship mostly had no image of God, but popular religion varied.
b: Unlike its neighbors, ancient Israel seems to have had no cult statue of its God; even the ark was an empty throne between cherubim (25:17–22). Excavated Israelite shrines, such as the one at Arad (800s–700s BC), held standing stones and altars but no statue of a god. Tryggve Mettinger calls this "aniconism" and argues it is older than the written law. Yet there were exceptions: the golden calves of Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:28), the bronze serpent worshiped until Hezekiah broke it (2 Kings 18:4), and drawings and inscriptions at Kuntillet Ajrud (about 800 BC) that mention "YHWH and his Asherah." The three zones (sky, earth, waters below) list everything in creation, as in Genesis 1.

a: I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God
p: Qanna, "jealous," is used only of God. It is the jealousy of a faithful husband, not petty envy.
b: Qanna describes God alone (34:14, "the LORD's name is Jealous"; Deuteronomy 4:24; Deuteronomy 5:9). The related noun qin'ah can mean jealousy, zeal or passion. The prophets explain it with the image of marriage: worshiping other gods is adultery against a husband who loves his wife (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). The point is not insecurity but exclusive love: a love that would not care whether its partner was faithful would not be love. Paul speaks of a "godly jealousy" for the church as a bride (2 Corinthians 11:2), and James 4:5 speaks of God's longing for the spirit he placed in us.
orig: אֵל קַנָּא (El qanna), "a jealous God"
r: 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24; Deuteronomy 6:15; Joshua 24:19; Nahum 1:2; Hosea 2:16–20; 2 Corinthians 11:2; James 4:5

a: I bring the fathers' guilt home to the children, to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me
p: Other passages say each person dies for his own sin. Jewish and Christian readers have explained the tension.
b: Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18:20 insist that children are not put to death for their parents, and Jeremiah 31:29–30 rejects the proverb about sour grapes. How does this verse fit? The Talmud (Berakhot 7a) and Targum Onqelos answer that it applies only when the children "hold on to their fathers' deeds": the phrase "of those who hate me" describes the children. Others note that three or four generations could live in one household, so the verse may describe how a family's sin harms everyone under its roof. Christian readers have connected it with inherited sin (Romans 5:12) and with Jesus' rejection of blaming a blind man's parents (John 9:2–3).
orig: פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבֹת עַל־בָּנִים עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁים וְעַל־רִבֵּעִים לְשֹׂנְאָי (poqed avon avot al-banim...)

a: but I show loyal love to thousands
p: The contrast is lopsided on purpose: three or four generations against thousands.
b: The Hebrew says la'alafim, "to thousands." Deuteronomy 7:9 spells out "to a thousand generations," and many translations read that sense here, so the contrast is three or four generations of punishment against a thousand of loyal love. Either way, God's mercy far outweighs his judgment, and 34:6–7 repeats the formula in a fuller form. Chesed is the faithful, generous love that keeps a covenant (see the topic hesed); this site renders it "loyal love."
orig: וְעֹשֶׂה חֶסֶד לַאֲלָפִים (ve'oseh chesed la'alafim), "doing loyal love to thousands"

a: You must not take up the name of the LORD your God for something empty.
p: The command is about more than swearing. It may forbid false oaths, magic, or carrying God's name falsely.
b: The verb nasa means "lift, carry," and shav means "emptiness, falsehood." Most ancient readers took the command to forbid false or careless oaths in God's name (Leviticus 19:12; the Mekhilta; Philo), and Jesus' teaching on oaths builds on it (Matthew 5:33–37). Others extend it to using God's name in magic or curses, or to any light use of it. Carmen Imes (2018) argued that "carrying" the name is like the high priest wearing it on his forehead (28:36–38): Israel bears God's name before the world and must not do so emptily. Out of reverence for this command and Leviticus 24:16, Jews stopped pronouncing the name YHWH, saying Adonai or HaShem ("the Name") instead.
orig: לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת־שֵׁם־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא (lo tissa et-shem-YHWH Eloheikha lashav)
r: Leviticus 19:12; Leviticus 24:15–16; Deuteronomy 5:11; Deuteronomy 28:36–38; Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12

a: Remember the day of the Sabbath
p: Exodus says "remember" the Sabbath; Deuteronomy says "keep" it. The rabbis said God spoke both at once.
b: Deuteronomy 5:12 begins the Sabbath command with shamor, "keep, guard," instead of zakhor, "remember." The rabbis taught that "remember" and "keep" were spoken in a single utterance, something no human mouth could do (Shevuot 20b; Mekhilta). The sixteenth-century Sabbath hymn Lekha Dodi, sung on Friday evenings, opens with that idea. In Jewish practice "remember" became the positive duty, such as the blessing over wine (Kiddush), and "keep" the duty to refrain from work. "Remember" also suggests the Sabbath was already known (16:23–30).
orig: זָכוֹר אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת (zakhor et-yom hashabbat)

a: not your slave, man or woman, not your animals, not the foreigner who lives in your towns
p: No other ancient people had a weekly rest day for all, including slaves and animals.
b: The Sabbath includes those who had no rights to rest: slaves, foreign workers and even work animals. Scholars once looked for its origin in Babylon, where the fifteenth day of the month (the full moon) was called shapattu and certain days (the 7th, 14th, 19th, 21st and 28th) were considered unlucky for some activities. But those days followed the moon, applied mostly to the king and priests, and were not days of rest for everyone. Most scholars now conclude that the weekly Sabbath, cut loose from the moon and given to the whole household, has no real parallel in the ancient world. Deuteronomy 5:14–15 adds the reason: "Then your slave, man or woman, can rest just as you do. Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt."

a: and on the seventh day he rested
p: Exodus grounds the Sabbath in creation, Deuteronomy in the escape from Egypt.
b: The reason given here points back to Genesis 2:2–3, which in this site's Plain English reads: "On the seventh day God finished the work he had been doing, and on the seventh day he rested from all the work he had been doing. God blessed the seventh day and set it apart as holy." In Exodus 31:17 God even "stopped and caught his breath." In Deuteronomy 5:15 the reason is different: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt." Many readers see the two as one idea: the Sabbath honors God as Creator and as Rescuer, and it trains a freed people not to become slave drivers. The verb here is vayyanach, "he settled, rested," related to the name Noah.
orig: וַיָּנַח בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי (vayyanach bayyom hashevi'i)
r: 31:17; Genesis 2:2–3; Deuteronomy 5:15; Acts 4:24; Acts 14:15; Revelation 14:7; Hebrews 4:4, 9–10

a: That is why the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy.
p: Jews keep the seventh day. Most Christians worship on Sunday. Some keep both, or neither as law.
b: Judaism keeps the Sabbath from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. The first Christians met on "the first day of the week" (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), the day of the resurrection, which Revelation 1:10 may call "the Lord's Day." Over time most churches came to treat Sunday as the Christian day of rest and worship; Thomas Aquinas taught that the moral core of the commandment (setting time aside for God) remains while the choice of day was ceremonial. The Reformed Westminster tradition calls Sunday "the Christian Sabbath." Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday, citing this verse. Others read Colossians 2:16–17 and Hebrews 4:9–10 to mean that the Sabbath rest is fulfilled in Christ.
r: Mark 2:27–28; Acts 20:7; Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10; Revelation 1:10

a: Honor your father and your mother
p: "Honor" is the verb "make heavy." Paul calls this the first commandment with a promise.
b: Kabbed means "give weight to," the same root as "glory" (see 16:7). Its opposite is qalal, "treat as light," the word for "curse" in 21:17. Leviticus 19:3 names the mother first. The rabbis said there are three partners in making a person, God, father and mother, and that honoring parents honors God (Kiddushin 30b). Jesus defends this command against a practice that let people dedicate to the temple money owed to aged parents (Mark 7:9–13). Ephesians 6:2–3 calls it "the first commandment with a promise" and quotes the longer Greek wording: "so that it may go well with you" (see the variant).
orig: כַּבֵּד אֶת־אָבִיךָ וְאֶת־אִמֶּךָ (kabbed et-avikha ve'et-immekha)

a: You must not murder.
p: The KJV's "Thou shalt not kill" is broader than the Hebrew ratsach, which never covers war and almost never execution.
b: Hebrew has several verbs for killing. Ratsach, used here, is never used for killing in war and almost never for a lawful execution (but see Numbers 35:27, 30), though the same law commands both (21:12; 32:27). It is used for murder and also for accidental killing, which is why Numbers 35 calls the man who flees to a city of refuge a rotseach even when he did not mean to kill. So "murder" fits most uses, though not all. Christians differ over how far the command reaches: the Catholic Church applies it to abortion and euthanasia and now teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible (2018), while pacifist traditions (Mennonites, Quakers) apply it to war. Jesus extends it to anger and insult (Matthew 5:21–22).
orig: לֹא תִּרְצָח (lo tirtsach)
r: 21:12–14; Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:11–31; Numbers 35:27–30; Deuteronomy 19:4–6; Matthew 5:21–22; Romans 13:9; 1 John 3:15

a: You must not commit adultery.
p: In Israel's law, adultery meant sex with another man's wife. The order of these three commands varies.
b: Na'af referred to sex between a married or engaged woman and a man not her husband (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24). A married man's affair with an unmarried woman was treated differently (see 22:16–17), a double standard the prophets begin to question when they hold men to account (Malachi 2:14–16). Jesus extends the command to lustful looking (Matthew 5:27–28) and rejects easy divorce (Matthew 19:3–9). The order of 20:13–15 also varies in early witnesses: the Nash Papyrus, Philo, Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9 and James 2:11 put adultery before murder, and the Septuagint of Exodus in Codex Vaticanus is usually reported to read adultery, theft, murder.
r: Leviticus 18:20; Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24; Proverbs 6:32; Malachi 2:14–16; Matthew 5:27–28; Luke 18:20; Romans 13:9; James 2:11

a: You must not steal.
p: The rabbis read this command as kidnapping, since its neighbors carry the death penalty.
b: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 86a) and the Mekhilta reason that the command is known by its company: murder and adultery carry the death penalty, so this "stealing" must also be a capital crime, namely kidnapping a person (21:16). Ordinary theft of property is covered by Leviticus 19:11, "do not steal," in the plural. Most Christian traditions read the command broadly, as forbidding every kind of theft, including cheating workers of wages and dishonest trade (Luther's Large Catechism; Ephesians 4:28).
orig: לֹא תִּגְנֹב (lo tignov)

a: as a lying witness
p: The command speaks of testimony in court. Deuteronomy says "an empty witness."
b: Ed shaqer is literally "a witness of falsehood," and the verb anah, "answer, testify," places the command in a courtroom, where a false witness could cost a neighbor his land or his life (1 Kings 21:10–13; Deuteronomy 19:16–21, where the false witness receives the punishment he intended). Deuteronomy 5:20 reads ed shav, "an empty witness." Christian teaching has applied the command to every kind of lie and to protecting a neighbor's good name; Luther's Small Catechism says it means to "defend him, speak well of him, and explain everything in the kindest way."
orig: לֹא־תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר (lo-ta'aneh vere'akha ed shaqer)

a: You must not crave your neighbor's house.
t: Coveting: a feeling or a scheme?
p: Chamad means to desire something so that one moves to take it. Did the command forbid feelings or acts?
b: The verb chamad is often followed by taking: "I craved them and took them" (Joshua 7:21); "they covet fields and seize them" (Micah 2:2). On that basis some scholars argue that the command forbids schemes to get what belongs to another. Maimonides drew the line within Jewish law: one breaks "do not covet" only by acting to obtain the thing, and Deuteronomy's added "do not desire" (lo titavveh) forbids the inner craving itself (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Robbery and Lost Property 1:9–10). Paul read it as a command about desire: "I would not have known craving if the law had not said, You must not crave" (Romans 7:7). It is the only one of the ten that reaches inside the heart. "House" here likely means the whole household, listed afterward.
orig: לֹא תַחְמֹד בֵּית רֵעֶךָ (lo tachmod beit re'ekha)
r: Deuteronomy 5:21; Deuteronomy 7:25; Joshua 7:21; Micah 2:2; Romans 7:7–8; Romans 13:9; Luke 12:15

a: All the people were seeing the thunder
p: The Hebrew says the people "saw the voices." Rabbi Akiva said they saw what is heard.
b: The verb is "seeing" for everything: the qolot ("voices," thunder), the torches of lightning, the sound of the horn and the smoking mountain. Translations usually add "heard." Rabbi Akiva taught that at Sinai Israel "saw what is heard" (Mekhilta), and Philo said the voice of God became visible flame (On the Decalogue 46–47). The word for lightning, lappidim, means torches, the same word as the burning torch that passed between the pieces when God made his covenant with Abram (Genesis 15:17).
orig: וְכָל־הָעָם רֹאִים אֶת־הַקּוֹלֹת (vekhol-ha'am ro'im et-haqqolot)

a: Let it be you who speaks with us
t: A go-between, and a prophet like Moses
p: The people's fear makes Moses their mediator. Deuteronomy turns it into the promise of a prophet like Moses.
b: Deuteronomy 5:23–31 tells this scene at length, and God approves the people's request: "Everything they have said is right" (Deuteronomy 5:28). Deuteronomy 18:15–18 then roots the promise of a future "prophet like me" in this very day at Horeb, when the people asked not to hear God's voice again. Peter and Stephen apply that promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37), and the Samaritan Pentateuch inserts it here (see the variant at 20:21). Hebrews 12:19 recalls that the hearers pleaded to hear nothing more. Paul calls Moses a mediator of the law (Galatians 3:19), and 1 Timothy 2:5 calls Christ the one mediator between God and humanity.
r: Deuteronomy 5:23–31; Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37–38; Galatians 3:19–20; 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 12:18–21

a: God has come to test you, and so that the fear of him will be before your faces
p: Moses says "do not fear" and then says God came so that his fear would stay with them. Two kinds of fear.
b: The same root, yare, appears in both halves: "Don't be afraid" and "his fear" (yir'ato). The first is panic that drives people away; the second is reverent awe that keeps them from sin. "The start of wisdom is the fear of the LORD" (Proverbs 9:10) means the second. "To put you to the test" (nassot) can also be heard as "to lift you up," from nes, "banner" (see 17:15); Rashi reads it as "to make you great" by revealing himself to you.
orig: אַל־תִּירָאוּ (al-tira'u), "do not fear"; יִרְאָתוֹ (yir'ato), "his fear"

a: the deep darkness where God was
p: Christian and Jewish mystics read Moses' entry into darkness as a picture of knowing God beyond knowledge.
b: Arafel is a heavy, dark cloud. Solomon recalls it at the temple's dedication: "The LORD has said / he will live in the thick dark cloud" (1 Kings 8:12), and the Psalms place it around God's throne (Psalm 18:11; Psalm 97:2). Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses (about 390) made this verse the center of Christian mystical theology: Moses first met God in light (the burning bush), then in cloud, then in darkness, because the nearer one comes to God the more one sees that he is beyond seeing. Pseudo-Dionysius, about a century later, spoke of the "divine darkness" beyond all light.
orig: הָעֲרָפֶל (ha'arafel), "the thick darkness"

a: You have seen for yourselves that I spoke with you from the heavens.
t: From heaven, or on the mountain?
p: God spoke "from the heavens," yet he came down on Sinai. Readers have explained how both are true.
b: Chapter 19 says the LORD came down on the mountain (19:11, 18, 20), but here he speaks "from the heavens." Deuteronomy 4:36 combines them: from heaven he made you hear his voice, and on earth he showed you his great fire. The Mekhilta resolves it by saying God bent the heavens down onto the mountain (Psalm 18:9, "He bent the sky low and came down"). Critical scholars often see two theologies: an older one of God coming down to a holy mountain, and the Deuteronomic one in which God stays in heaven and only his voice or name comes to earth. The verse opens the Covenant Code (20:22–23:33).

a: Do not make anything to set beside me
p: The Hebrew is compressed: "Do not make with me; gods of silver and gods of gold do not make."
b: The sentence reads literally: "Do not make with me; gods of silver and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves." The first clause may mean "do not make (images) to stand beside me," or "do not make (gods) along with me," or, as the Masoretic punctuation suggests, "do not make (anything) with me: gods of silver..." Rashi applied it even to the gold cherubim: they must not be made of silver, or more than two. The warning immediately after God speaks "from the heavens" makes the point of Deuteronomy 4:15: you saw no form, so make none. Israel breaks this very command in chapter 32.
orig: לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן אִתִּי (lo ta'asun itti), "do not make with me"

a: Make me an altar of earth
p: Israel's first altars were to be heaps of earth or uncut stones, nothing like the grand altars of temples.
b: An altar of packed earth or rough fieldstones was simple, local and cheap. Joshua 8:30–31 builds such an altar on Mount Ebal and quotes 20:25. Archaeologists have found altars of earth and uncut stones in Israelite levels, such as the altar in the shrine at Arad, and a stone structure on Mount Ebal that its excavator, Adam Zertal, identified as Joshua's altar (others think it a watchtower or farmhouse). The rule contrasts with the bronze altar of the tabernacle (27:1–8) and the great altars of Solomon's temple, which some read as a deliberate move from the simple to the grand.

a: In every place where I make my name remembered
p: This law allows altars "in every place." Deuteronomy 12 allows sacrifice only at the one place God chooses.
b: Deuteronomy 12:5–14 commands Israel to bring sacrifices only to "the place the LORD will choose" and to stop sacrificing "in every place you see." Critical scholars read this verse as older law, from a time when altars stood at many local shrines (Shechem, Bethel, Shiloh, Gibeon), and Deuteronomy as the later reform of King Josiah, who closed the local shrines (2 Kings 23).
