Traditional readers answer that the two laws fit different periods: in the wilderness and before the temple, God's name was "remembered" wherever the ark or tabernacle stood. The Samaritan Pentateuch reads "in the place," singular and past tense, pointing to one chosen site (see the variant).
r: Deuteronomy 12:5–14; Joshua 22:10–29; 1 Samuel 7:17; 1 Kings 3:2–4; 1 Kings 18:30; 2 Kings 23:8–9

a: If you have swung your blade over it
p: The word for tool is cherev, "sword." The rabbis said iron, which shortens life, may not touch the altar.
b: Hebrew cherev normally means "sword" and only here and a few places a cutting tool. The rabbis drew a lesson: the altar was made to lengthen life and iron was made to shorten it, so it is not right for the one to be lifted over the other (Mishnah Middot 3:4; Mekhilta; Rashi). The stones of the second temple's altar were said to be untouched by iron, and 1 Kings 6:7 says the stones of Solomon's temple were dressed at the quarry so that no iron tool was heard at the site. Rashi adds a further lesson: the altar makes peace between Israel and God, so if stones that cannot see or hear are protected from iron for that reason, how much more will a person who makes peace between people be protected from harm.
orig: חַרְבְּךָ הֵנַפְתָּ (charbekha henafta), "you have waved your sword"

a: do not go up to my altar by steps
p: Men in the ancient world often wore short kilts. Later the priests were given linen undergarments.
b: Climbing steps in a short kilt would expose the body, and the law guards the sanctuary from anything like the sexual rites known in some ancient worship. Later the priests were ordered to wear linen undergarments (28:42–43), and the great altar was approached by a ramp; the Mishnah describes the ramp of the second temple altar (Middot 3:3). Ezekiel's vision of a future altar has steps (Ezekiel 43:17), which suggests that by then priests' clothing had made the issue disappear. Rashi drew a moral from this verse too: if one must not show disrespect even to stones, how much more must one respect a fellow human being, made in the image of the Creator.

a: Here are the rulings you will lay before them.
p: The laws of 20:22–23:33 resemble older law collections from Mesopotamia, above all the Laws of Hammurabi.
b: Scholars call 20:22–23:33 the Covenant Code, after "the scroll of the covenant" in 24:7. Many of its laws are written "if... then," like the law collections of Ur-Nammu (about 2100 BC), Eshnunna (about 1800 BC) and Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC), copies of which were still studied centuries later. Some laws are strikingly close (see 21:22, 21:28–32 and 21:35). Most scholars think Israel shared a common legal tradition of the region; David Wright (2009) argues the Covenant Code was written directly from Hammurabi's text, others (Raymond Westbrook, Bernard Jackson) see shared custom and scribal training. The differences matter too: God, not a king, gives these laws; penalties do not change with social class; and no property crime is punished by death.
orig: וְאֵלֶּה הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים (ve'elleh hammishpatim), "and these are the rulings"

a: the rulings
p: Some laws are cases ("if someone..."), others are flat commands ("You must not..."). Both appear here.
b: In 1934 Albrecht Alt distinguished "casuistic" law, which states a case and its penalty ("If a man gets into a fight..."), from "apodictic" law, which commands without conditions ("You must not murder"). The mishpatim (rulings) of 21:1–22:17 are mostly case law, like the law codes of Israel's neighbors; the rest of the Covenant Code (22:18–23:19) shifts to commands, often with motives ("for you were foreigners in Egypt"). Alt thought apodictic law was distinctively Israelite; later study found it elsewhere too, but the blend of case law, command and appeal to God's character remains typical of Israel's law.
orig: הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים (hammishpatim), "the rulings"

a: If you acquire a Hebrew slave
p: These "slaves" were mostly Israelites sold for debt, freed after six years. Other laws treat foreigners differently.
b: A "Hebrew slave" was usually someone who sold himself, or was sold, to pay a debt or a theft (22:3; 2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:5). Hammurabi's laws (§117) free a family member sold for debt after three years; this law sets six, with the seventh year as a Sabbath of release. Deuteronomy 15:12–18 extends the release to women and requires the master to send the slave off with gifts. Leviticus 25:39–46 goes further: an Israelite must not be treated as a slave at all but as a hired worker until the Jubilee, while foreign slaves could be held for life. Jeremiah 34:8–22 condemns Jerusalem's leaders for freeing their slaves and then taking them back. The word "Hebrew" may have meant a social class as well as a people (see the topic on slavery).
orig: עֶבֶד עִבְרִי (eved ivri), "a Hebrew slave"

a: the woman and her children remain with her master
p: The freed man must leave behind the wife and children his master gave him. Readers have not hidden from this.
b: The law assumes the wife given by the master was herself a slave, probably for life, so she and her children remain the master's property. The freed man must choose between freedom and his family, which is what 21:5–6 addresses. Some defenders note that the law at least lets him stay with them; others say the choice itself is a form of pressure that turned temporary slaves into permanent ones. Many modern readers, Jewish and Christian, see in laws like this the Torah limiting a cruel institution it did not abolish, a step on a road that later readers pressed further. Others think it simply reflects the values of its age. See the chapter page on reading the slavery laws honestly.

a: his master is to bring him to God
p: Ha-Elohim can mean God at the sanctuary, or the judges. The KJV and Jewish tradition say "judges."
b: Ha-Elohim normally means "God," but Targum Onqelos, Rashi and the KJV translate "the judges" here and in 22:8–9, since judges stand in God's place (Psalm 82:1, 6, where God calls human rulers elohim, a verse Jesus quotes in John 10:34–35). Others think of a sanctuary where the act was done before God, or of household gods kept near the door, as some ancient Near Eastern texts suggest. Deuteronomy 15:17 sets the ceremony at "the door" of the house and does not mention God. The Plain English keeps "God" and leaves the question open.
orig: אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים (el-ha'Elohim), "to God" or "to the judges"

a: his master will pierce his ear with an awl
p: The Talmud says the ear that heard "they are my slaves" at Sinai, and chose a human master, is marked.
b: The pierced ear was a visible sign of permanent service. The Talmud explains why the ear in particular: "The ear that heard at Mount Sinai, 'For the Israelites are slaves to me' (Leviticus 25:55), and not slaves of slaves, and yet went and acquired a master for itself, let it be pierced" (Kiddushin 22b; Rashi). The doorpost recalls the doorposts marked with blood at the Passover (12:7, 22). Psalm 40:6, "ears you have dug for me," may echo the custom, and the Greek of that psalm is quoted in Hebrews 10:5 of Christ's obedience.

a: for life
p: Le'olam means "forever" or "for life." The rabbis said it ended at the Jubilee.
b: Le'olam usually means "for all time," but of a person it means for the rest of life (1 Samuel 1:22; 1 Samuel 27:12). The rabbis, reading this law together with Leviticus 25:40, which frees Israelite servants in the Jubilee year, ruled that "forever" here lasts until the next Jubilee or the master's death (Mekhilta; Rashi). The Plain English "for life" gives the plain sense of this verse taken alone.
orig: לְעֹלָם (le'olam), "forever"

a: If a man sells his daughter as a slave woman
p: These verses protect a girl sold into a household as a future wife. They also show how women could be sold.
b: The amah here is not a laborer released after six years but a girl sold as a future wife or concubine for the master or his son (21:8–9). Poor families sold children under debt; Hammurabi's laws (§117) mention wives and children sold for debt, and Nehemiah 5:5 describes Israelite daughters forced into such sales. The law gives the girl real protections: she must be bought back if rejected, cannot be sold to foreigners, must be treated as a daughter if given to a son, and goes free if her food, clothing and marital rights are cut (21:8–11). The rabbis limited the sale to a girl under twelve and said she went free when she reached puberty (Mekhilta; Rashi). Many modern readers still find the arrangement itself a sign of how little power girls had.

a: her rights as a wife
p: The third right, onah, is rare. The rabbis said it means marital relations; others say oil or a home.
b: She'er is food (literally "flesh"), kesut clothing, and onah a word found only here. The rabbis took it as the wife's right to sexual relations, from a root meaning "time" or "season," and the Mishnah even sets minimum frequencies by the husband's occupation (Ketubot 5:6; Ketubot 47b–48a). Shalom Paul and others note that Mesopotamian texts list food, oil and clothing as a wife's basic support, and suggest "oil" here; still others suggest "lodging," from a word for "dwelling." Paul's teaching that husband and wife owe each other their marital duty (1 Corinthians 7:3–5) has a similar spirit to the rabbinic view.
orig: שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ (she'erah kesutah ve'onatah)

a: Whoever hits someone and he dies must be put to death.
p: Murder is the one crime that cannot be paid off with money. The rule goes back to Genesis 9:6.
b: The formula mot yumat, "he must surely be put to death," marks the capital laws of 21:12–17. The principle is old: in this site's Plain English, Genesis 9:6 says, "Whoever spills a human's blood, by a human his blood will be spilled, for in God's image he made humankind." Numbers 35:31 adds that no ransom may be taken for a murderer's life. Moshe Greenberg (1960) argued that this is the heart of biblical criminal law: unlike Babylonian law, which could punish theft with death and let some killings be paid off, Israel's law treats human life as beyond price and property as never worth a life.
orig: מוֹת יוּמָת (mot yumat), "he must surely be put to death"

a: and God brought it about by his hand
t: An act of God, and a place of refuge
p: An accidental killing is described as something God let happen. Later law sets up cities of refuge.
b: Hebrew calls an accident something that "God let meet his hand," much as English speaks of an "act of God." The killer is not a murderer, but the victim's family may still seek blood, so God promises "a place" to flee. Numbers 35, Deuteronomy 19 and Joshua 20 develop this into six cities of refuge. The Talmud adds a striking story: God arranges for a man who murdered in secret and a man who killed by accident in secret to meet at the same inn, where the second falls from a ladder onto the first, so that justice is done to both (Makkot 10b).
orig: וְהָאֱלֹהִים אִנָּה לְיָדוֹ (veha'Elohim innah leyado), "and God let it meet his hand"

a: take him away even from my altar to die
t: No refuge at the altar for a murderer
p: In the ancient world a fugitive could cling to an altar for protection. Not a deliberate killer.
b: Many ancient temples offered asylum: a fugitive who grasped the altar could not be touched. In 1 Kings 1:50–53 Adonijah holds the horns of the altar and Solomon spares him; in 1 Kings 2:28–34 Joab does the same, and Solomon has him killed there, citing his murders. This verse is the law behind that story: the altar protects the innocent, not the one who kills "by cunning." The verb zid, "act presumptuously," is the same one used of Egypt's arrogance in 18:11.

a: Anyone who strikes his father or his mother must be put to death.
t: Were these death penalties carried out?
p: The rabbis narrowed capital laws so much that executions became very rare.
b: Hammurabi's laws (§195) cut off the hand of a son who strikes his father. Here the penalty is death, and the rabbis limited it to a blow that draws blood (Sanhedrin 84b). The Mishnah shows how reluctant Jewish courts became: a court that executed once in seven years was called "destructive"; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah said, "or once in seventy years"; and Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva said that if they had sat on the court, no one would ever have been executed (Makkot 1:10). The Talmud says the law of the rebellious son (Deuteronomy 21:18–21) "never happened and never will" (Sanhedrin 71a). Christians differ on whether these penalties teach anything for modern states.

a: Whoever steals a person must be put to death
p: Kidnapping to sell a person was a capital crime. Abolitionists quoted this verse against the slave trade.
b: Joseph was the Bible's most famous victim of this crime: "I was stolen away, stolen from the land of the Hebrews" (Genesis 40:15, in this site's Plain English). Deuteronomy 24:7 restates the law for kidnapping a fellow Israelite, and the Greek Septuagint here adds "one of the sons of Israel," as in Deuteronomy (the Greek also places this law after the law about cursing parents). Paul lists "man-stealers" (andrapodistai) among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). In the 1700s and 1800s, abolitionists in Britain and America used this verse to argue that the Atlantic slave trade, built on kidnapping, was condemned by God's law, while defenders of slavery appealed to other verses (see the topic on slavery).

a: Anyone who curses his father or his mother
p: The verb qalal, "curse," means "treat as light," the opposite of "honor" (make heavy).
b: Meqallel comes from qalal, "to be light," the exact opposite of kabbed, "to make heavy, honor," in 20:12. To "curse" a parent is to treat them as worthless, often by calling down harm on them in God's name. Leviticus 20:9 repeats the law, and Jesus quotes it against those who used religious vows to avoid supporting their parents (Matthew 15:4; Mark 7:10). The Greek Septuagint has "speaks evil of."
orig: וּמְקַלֵּל (umeqallel), "and whoever curses"
r: 20:12; Leviticus 19:3; Leviticus 20:9; Proverbs 20:20; Proverbs 30:11; Matthew 15:4; Mark 7:10

a: He only pays for the time the man lost and sees that he is fully healed.
t: Paying for an injury, and the duty to heal
p: The rabbis built a whole system of injury compensation, and a license for doctors, on this verse.
b: Jewish law lists five payments for injuring someone: for the damage itself, pain, medical costs, lost work and humiliation (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1). Two of them come straight from this verse: shivto, "his sitting," meaning lost time, and rappo yerappe, "he shall surely have him healed," meaning medical costs. The Talmud also drew from the doubled verb rappo yerappe that "permission is given to the physician to heal" (Bava Kamma 85a), answering those who thought medicine interfered with God's decrees. The walking stick shows the man has recovered enough to go about.
orig: רַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא (rappo yerappe), "he shall surely heal"

a: the death must be avenged
p: A master who beat a slave to death was punished. Most ancient law treated a slave's death as property loss.
b: Babylonian law usually treated injury to someone else's slave as damage to the owner's property, paid to the owner (Hammurabi §§199, 213–214). This law protects the slave from his own master: if the slave dies under the rod, "he must surely be avenged" (naqom yinnaqem). The Mekhilta and Rashi say this means the death penalty by the sword. Others think the penalty was left to the court. Together with 21:26–27, where an injured slave goes free, these are among the strongest protections for slaves in ancient law. They do not remove the master's right to beat a slave, which the next verse assumes.
orig: נָקֹם יִנָּקֵם (naqom yinnaqem), "he must surely be avenged"

a: because the slave is his money
t: "His money": reading the slavery laws honestly
p: This phrase shows plainly that the law treats a slave as property. Readers respond in different ways.
b: If the slave lives a day or two, the master is not punished, "for he is his silver." Some explain that the delay shows the master did not intend to kill, and that his loss is penalty enough (Mekhilta). But the phrase is plain: the law thinks of a slave as purchased property. In the American debates over slavery, defenders quoted this verse; abolitionists such as Frederick Douglass answered from the Bible's larger themes of the exodus and the image of God. Many Jewish and Christian scholars today (Paul Copan, for example) say the Torah accepted slavery as a fact of the ancient economy while setting it on a path toward limits, release and dignity (20:10; 21:26–27; Deuteronomy 23:15–16; Job 31:13–15). Others, such as Hector Avalos, say the text should not be defended at all on this point. This site states the text as it is.
orig: כִּי כַסְפּוֹ הוּא (ki khaspo hu), "for he is his money"

a: and her children come out, but no harm follows
p: Does this law describe a miscarriage or a premature live birth? The answer has been used in debates on abortion.
b: The Hebrew says "her children come out and there is no ason (harm)." (1) Most Jewish interpreters and most critical scholars read a miscarriage: the fine pays for the lost fetus, and "harm" means injury to the woman, the view of the Mekhilta and Rashi; Hammurabi (§§209–214) and Hittite law likewise fine for causing a miscarriage. (2) Many evangelical scholars read a premature birth: yatsa, "come out," is used of live births (Genesis 25:25–26), and "harm" may cover mother or child, so the child's life is protected like the mother's (so the NIV of 2011). (3) The Greek Septuagint makes a different law: a fine if the child was not yet "formed," life for life if it was (see the variant). That reading shaped Christian teaching from Augustine on. On how the verse is used in the abortion debate, see the chapter page.
orig: וְיָצְאוּ יְלָדֶיהָ וְלֹא יִהְיֶה אָסוֹן (veyatse'u yeladeha velo yihyeh ason)

a: as the arbiters decide
p: The last word is rare. It may mean judges, a court's assessment, or a sum fixed by estimate.
b: Biflilim occurs only a few times (Deuteronomy 32:31; Job 31:11). Older Jewish and Christian readers took it as "by the judges" (Targum Onqelos, Rashi, KJV), which would let a court check the husband's demand. E. A. Speiser argued for "by reckoning" or "as assessed," meaning a fair estimate rather than whatever the husband wanted. Some scholars have proposed correcting the text. All readings agree that the fine was not left to private revenge.
orig: בִּפְלִלִים (biflilim), "by arbiters" or "by assessment"

a: eye for eye
t: The "law of retaliation" in the ancient world
p: Hammurabi's laws also say "eye for eye," but only between equals. The Torah applies one rule to all.
b: Scholars call this principle the lex talionis, Latin for "law of retaliation." Hammurabi's laws state it: if a man of the upper class destroys the eye of another such man, his own eye is destroyed (§196), but for a commoner's eye he pays a mina of silver, and for a slave's eye half the slave's price (§§198–199). In the Torah the same measure applies to all, "one law for foreigner and native-born alike" (Leviticus 24:22), and the only class distinction is that a master who injures his own slave sets the slave free (21:26–27). Many historians think talion was a step forward in its day: it replaced blood feud and unlimited revenge (compare Lamech's boast of seventy-sevenfold vengeance in Genesis 4:23–24) with a limit.

a: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
p: The rabbis ruled that "eye for eye" means the value of an eye. No Jewish court took eyes.
b: The Mekhilta and the Talmud (Bava Kamma 83b–84a) argue at length that "eye for eye" means monetary payment equal to the loss. Among the reasons: a literal law could not be applied fairly (what of a man with one eye, or a blind man who blinds someone?), Numbers 35:31 forbids ransom only for a murderer, implying ransom is allowed for injuries, and the next words, "burn for burn, cut for cut," are impossible to measure exactly in the body. Josephus says the injured person could accept money instead (Antiquities 4.280). So Jewish law has paid compensation for injuries since antiquity. Maimonides adds that the wording shows what the offender deserves, even though the court collects money (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Wounding and Damaging 1:3–6).
orig: עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן שֵׁן תַּחַת שֵׁן (ayin tachat ayin shen tachat shen)

a: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
p: Jesus quotes this law and tells his followers not to retaliate. Christians differ on what he meant.
b: In Matthew 5:38–42 Jesus says, "You have heard what was said: 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.' But I myself tell you: do not set yourself against the evil person," and he gives examples: turn the other cheek, give up your outer robe too, go the second mile. Readers take this in several ways. Some (Tolstoy, Mennonites and other peace churches) read a complete rejection of force. Augustine and Luther distinguished personal revenge, which Jesus forbids, from the work of courts and rulers, which still punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). Many scholars note that the Torah itself already forbade private revenge (Leviticus 19:18) and that Jesus moves from the limit of justice to the generosity of love, a point Jewish teachers also made about going beyond the letter of the law (lifnim mishurat hadin).
r: Matthew 5:38–42; Luke 6:27–31; Leviticus 19:18; Romans 12:17–21; Romans 13:3–4; Proverbs 20:22; Proverbs 24:29

a: he must let the slave go free in exchange for the eye
p: If a master knocks out a slave's eye or tooth, the slave goes free. The rabbis extended it to 24 body parts.
b: The same word "in exchange for" (tachat) as in "eye for eye" is used here, but the payment is freedom. This rule has no known parallel in other ancient law collections, where only injury to another man's slave was compensated, and then to the owner. Even the loss of a tooth, a small injury, frees the slave, which suggests that any lasting injury counted. The rabbis applied it to the twenty-four "tips of the limbs," such as fingers, toes and ears (Kiddushin 24a–25a), but only for non-Israelite slaves, since Israelite servants went free in any case after six years.
orig: לַחָפְשִׁי יְשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ תַּחַת עֵינוֹ (lachofshi yeshallechennu tachat eino)

a: the ox must be stoned, and no one may eat its meat
p: Several older law codes also deal with an ox that gores. Only the Bible stones the ox itself.
b: The goring ox was a standard case in ancient law: the Laws of Eshnunna (§§53–55) and of Hammurabi (§§250–252) both treat it, and like the Bible they distinguish a first attack from an ox known to be dangerous whose owner was warned. The similarity is close enough that most scholars see a shared legal tradition. But only the Bible orders the ox stoned and its meat thrown away. J. J. Finkelstein argued this treats the ox as guilty of a crime against the order of creation: the animal has shed human blood, and God says in Genesis 9:5, in this site's Plain English, "From every animal I will demand it." Human life, again, is more than property.

a: If a ransom is set for him instead
p: A negligent owner could pay a kofer, a ransom, to save his life. The same idea stands behind Mark 10:45.
b: A kofer is a payment that buys back a life forfeited by law. Because the owner did not mean to kill, the victim's family may accept a ransom instead of his death, unlike a deliberate murderer, for whom no ransom is allowed (Numbers 35:31). The Greek Septuagint uses lytra, "ransom," here, and Jesus uses the related word when he says the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). Psalm 49:7–8 says no one can pay God the ransom for another's life. The census tax of 30:12 is also called a kofer.
orig: כֹּפֶר (kofer), "ransom"

a: silver, thirty shekels
p: Thirty shekels was the price of a slave's life. Zechariah and Matthew use the same sum.
b: When an ox kills a slave, the owner pays the slave's master thirty shekels; Hammurabi's laws set twenty (§252, a third of a mina). In Zechariah 11:12–13 the prophet, playing a shepherd, is paid off with thirty pieces of silver and told to throw that "splendid price" to the potter. Matthew 26:15 says the chief priests paid Judas thirty pieces of silver to betray Jesus, and Matthew 27:9–10 links the sum to the prophets. Many readers see the point: Jesus was valued at the price of a slave. Joseph was sold for twenty pieces (Genesis 37:28).
orig: כֶּסֶף שְׁלֹשִׁים שְׁקָלִים (kesef sheloshim sheqalim), "thirty shekels of silver"

a: they are to sell the live ox and split the money, and split the dead one too
t: A law found almost word for word in Eshnunna
p: The Laws of Eshnunna, about 1800 BC, give the same ruling: the two owners share both oxen.
b: Law 53 of Eshnunna, a city in Mesopotamia, says that if an ox gores another ox and kills it, the two owners divide the price of the live ox and the value of the dead one. This is the closest parallel between biblical law and any other ancient text, and it shows that some cases were standard teaching material for scribes and judges across the region. Scholars disagree on how it reached Israel, whether through written copies (David Wright) or common legal custom (Raymond Westbrook). Either way, the Bible did not hide that some of its civil law was shared with other nations; it set it inside a covenant with God.

a: If someone steals an ox or a sheep
t: Different verse numbers in Hebrew Bibles
p: Hebrew Bibles number this verse 21:37. Every verse of chapter 22 is one number lower in Hebrew.
b: English Bibles, following the old Latin and Greek division, begin chapter 22 here. Printed Hebrew Bibles end chapter 21 with this verse (21:37), so English 22:2 is Hebrew 22:1, and so on to English 22:31 = Hebrew 22:30. Jewish translations such as the JPS follow the Hebrew numbers. This site uses the English numbering throughout; when a commentary or the Talmud cites "22:27," it may mean English 22:28.

a: he must repay with five cattle in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the sheep
t: Five for an ox, four for a sheep
p: Why more for an ox? The rabbis offered two answers, one about work and one about dignity.
b: A thief who still has the animal pays double (22:4), but one who has slaughtered or sold it pays four or five times, since he has gone further in his crime. Why five for an ox but four for a sheep? Rabbi Meir said the ox is worth more because it works the fields; Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai said God cares even for the dignity of a thief, who had to carry the sheep on his shoulder in shame and so pays less (Bava Kamma 79b; Mekhilta). David demands fourfold for the poor man's lamb in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:6), and Zacchaeus promises to repay fourfold (Luke 19:8). Hammurabi's law (§8) required thirtyfold or tenfold, or death if the thief could not pay.

a: If a thief is caught tunneling in
p: Killing a burglar at night is not murder; in daylight it is. The rabbis drew the principle of self-defense.
b: Houses were often built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through a wall (machteret, "digging through"); Jesus speaks of thieves who "dig through and steal" (Matthew 6:19–20; Matthew 24:43). At night the householder cannot know whether the intruder means to kill, so he is not guilty if the thief dies. Once "the sun has come up on him," things are different. The rabbis read the sun as a figure: if it is as clear as day that the thief does not mean to kill, killing him is murder (Mekhilta; Rashi). From this law the Talmud draws the rule, "If someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first" (Sanhedrin 72a).
orig: בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת (bammachteret), "in the breaking in"

a: he himself is sold to cover the theft
p: A thief who could not pay was sold as a debt slave. Jewish law later limited this sharply.
b: Since biblical law had no prisons, a thief who could not repay worked off the debt as a slave, under the six-year limit of 21:2. The rabbis limited the sale: only a man could be sold, and only for the value of what he stole, not the added penalty (Mekhilta; Rashi). Josephus reports that King Herod broke Jewish law by selling thieves to foreigners outside the country (Antiquities 16.1–5). The law is a reminder that "slavery" in these chapters is mostly an economic institution of debt.

a: If someone lets a field or vineyard be grazed bare
p: The verb ba'ar can mean "graze" or "burn." The next verse uses the same root for fire.
b: The verb yav'er and the noun be'iro ("his animals") come from roots that sound alike: one means "graze," another "burn." Most ancient and modern readers take this verse as grazing (Targum Onqelos; Rashi), and the next as fire. Some scholars read both verses as fire, since 22:6 calls the fire habbe'erah, from the "burn" root. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint have a longer verse that distinguishes partial and total damage (see the variant).
orig: יַבְעֶר־ (yav'er), "he lets graze" or "he burns"

a: If a fire goes out and finds thorns
p: Farmers burned thorns and stubble. A fire that spread was the farmer's responsibility.
b: Thornbushes along field edges burned fast (Psalm 58:9; Ecclesiastes 7:6). Samson burned the Philistines' grain by tying torches to foxes (Judges 15:4–5), and Absalom set Joab's barley field on fire to force a meeting (2 Samuel 14:30–31). The law holds the one who lit the fire fully responsible, even if he did not mean the damage, because fire is a known danger. Jewish law classed fire with the ox, the pit and the grazing animal as the four main kinds of damage (Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1), all from this part of Exodus.

a: the owner of the house is to be brought before God
p: As in 21:6, Elohim may mean God at the sanctuary or the judges. Here the verb in 22:9 is plural.
b: In 22:8–9 the case goes "to ha-Elohim," and in 22:9 "the one Elohim declares guilty" uses a plural verb (yarshi'un), which fits "the judges" better than "God." The KJV, Targum Onqelos and Rashi read "judges." Others think of a trial at the sanctuary by oath or by a sacred lot, as when Solomon prays that a person under suspicion who takes an oath before the altar may be judged by God (1 Kings 8:31–32). Either way, the judges act in God's name. See also 21:6 and 22:28.
orig: אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים (el-ha'Elohim), "to God" or "to the judges"

a: an oath by the LORD will settle it between the two of them
p: When there were no witnesses, a sworn oath before God ended the case. Hebrews says the same.
b: Ancient law often ended a case without evidence by having the accused swear before the god. Hammurabi's laws have a shepherd clear himself before the god when a lion kills an animal in the fold (§266), and a man whose deposit is lost swear his innocence (§§120, 249). The person taking the oath put himself under God's judgment, which ancient people feared deeply. Hebrews 6:16 states the principle: for people, an oath settles every dispute. The rabbis built on this verse the oath of the paid and unpaid guardian (Mishnah Shevuot; Bava Metzia 93a).

a: let him bring what is left as a witness
p: A shepherd showed the torn remains to prove a wild animal took the sheep. Amos uses the image for Israel.
b: Jacob complained to Laban that he had not been allowed even this defense; in this site's Plain English he says: "What wild animals tore I never brought to you. I took the loss myself" (Genesis 31:39). Amos 3:12 turns the custom into a grim picture: as a shepherd rescues from a lion's mouth two legs or a piece of an ear, so only scraps of Israel will be rescued. David told Saul of saving lambs from a lion and a bear (1 Samuel 17:34–35). The word for "torn" (terefah) returns in 22:31.
orig: יְבִאֵהוּ עֵד (yevi'ehu ed), "let him bring it as a witness"

a: If a man lures away a virgin who is not promised in marriage
p: This law treats seduction as a wrong to the father's household. It protects the woman's future, by its lights.
b: A virgin's father expected a bride-price (mohar) for her marriage (Genesis 34:12; 1 Samuel 18:25), and a woman who was no longer a virgin had poor prospects. The law forces the seducer to pay and to marry her, unless her father refuses, in which case he still pays (22:17). Defenders note that the law gives her support and gives her father, not the man, the final word. Critics note that it does not ask what she wants and treats the loss as her father's. Deuteronomy 22:28–29 deals with a man who "seizes" a girl, which many read as rape, and adds that he may never divorce her. Exodus 22:16 involves persuasion, not force.
orig: יְפַתֶּה (yefatteh), "entices, persuades"

a: A woman who works sorcery must not be left alive.
p: The KJV's "witch" has a tragic history. The Hebrew means a woman who practices harmful magic.
b: Mekhashefah is the feminine form of a word for a sorcerer who casts spells (7:11; Deuteronomy 18:10). The Greek Septuagint uses pharmakous, "poisoners, sorcerers." The rabbis said the feminine was used because women more often practiced sorcery, but applied the law to men and women alike (Sanhedrin 67a). The KJV's "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live" was quoted in the European and colonial witch trials of about 1450 to 1750, in which tens of thousands of people, most of them women, were executed, including twenty people at Salem in 1692. Historians stress that the ancient law dealt with harmful spells and poisoning in a world that believed in them, not with modern ideas of witchcraft.
orig: מְכַשֵּׁפָה לֹא תְחַיֶּה (mekhashefah lo techayyeh)

a: is to be put under the ban and destroyed
p: Cherem means something given over completely to God, often by destruction.
b: The verb yochoram comes from cherem, a thing devoted to God so totally that it can no longer be used by people; often that meant destruction (Leviticus 27:28–29; Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:17–21). Here the one who sacrifices to other gods becomes cherem. Deuteronomy 13:12–18 applies the same idea to a whole town that turns to idols. The Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to read "to other gods," making explicit what the Masoretic Text implies; the Plain English keeps the shorter text, "to the gods."
orig: יָחֳרָם (yochoram), "he shall be devoted to destruction"

a: for you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt
p: Israel's law protects the foreigner by appealing to Israel's own memory. The rabbis counted 36 such warnings.
b: A ger is a foreigner who lives among Israel without land or family protection. The law forbids both to "mistreat" him (yanah, wrong with words or prices, said the rabbis) and to "press" him (lachats, the very word for Egypt's oppression of Israel in 3:9). The reason is memory: you know what it is like (23:9). Leviticus 19:33–34 goes further: "love him as yourself." The Talmud reports that the Torah warns about the ger in thirty-six places, some say forty-six (Bava Metzia 59b). Later Jewish tradition often read ger as "convert," but the plain sense is a resident outsider. Jesus counts welcoming the stranger as welcoming him (Matthew 25:35).
orig: וְגֵר (veger), "and a foreigner"; תִלְחָצֶנּוּ (tilchatsennu), "press him"

a: Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly
t: God's own defense of the weak
p: God himself takes up the case of the widow and orphan. The verb is the one used for Egypt's affliction.
b: The verb anah, "afflict, treat harshly," is the word for what the Egyptians did to Israel (1:11–12). The pattern of the exodus repeats: if they cry out, God hears (3:7), and his anger burns. The punishment fits the crime: your own wives will become widows. The law then switches to the singular ("him... he cries"), which the rabbis read as covering anyone who is mistreated, not only widows and orphans (Mekhilta). Psalm 68:5 calls God "a father to orphans and a judge for widows," and James 1:27 says that pure religion means caring for orphans and widows when they suffer.
orig: תְעַנּוּן (te'annun), "you shall afflict"
r: 1:11–12; 3:7–9; Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 24:17; Deuteronomy 27:19; Psalm 68:5; Isaiah 1:17; James 1:27

a: Do not charge him interest
p: The Hebrew word for interest, neshekh, means a "bite." The ban shaped Jewish, Christian and Muslim law.
b: Neshekh comes from nashakh, "to bite": interest bites the borrower. In the ancient Near East interest on loans of silver often ran 20 percent a year and on grain about 33 percent (the Laws of Eshnunna §18A and Hammurabi set such limits). Loans to the poor were for survival, not business, so Israel's law forbids profiting from them (Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20, which allows interest from foreigners). The church long banned "usury": the Council of Nicaea (325) forbade clergy to lend at interest, and medieval law extended the ban; John Calvin argued in 1545 that moderate interest on business loans was allowed. Jewish law developed the heter iska, a partnership form, and Islam forbids riba.
orig: נֶשֶׁךְ (neshekh), "interest, bite"
r: Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Nehemiah 5:1–12; Psalm 15:5; Ezekiel 18:8, 13; Luke 6:34–35

a: give it back to him by sundown
t: A worker's coat, and a letter from 600 BC
p: A poor man's coat was his blanket. An ancient Hebrew letter shows a worker asking for his coat back.
b: The poor often had nothing to offer as security for a loan but their outer cloak, which served as a blanket at night (22:27). Deuteronomy 24:10–13 adds that the lender must wait outside for the pledge. Amos condemns those who lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge (Amos 2:8). An ostracon (inscribed potsherd) found in 1960 at Mesad Hashavyahu, near Yavneh-Yam on the coast, records the appeal of a field worker, about 630–600 BC, to an official: his garment has been taken by an overseer, and he asks for it back. It is a rare glimpse of this law, or the custom behind it, in daily life.
r: Deuteronomy 24:10–13, 17; Amos 2:8; Job 22:6; Job 24:9–10; Proverbs 20:16; Ezekiel 18:7

a: for I am gracious
p: Channun, "gracious," describes God. It returns in God's great self-description in 34:6.
b: Channun describes one who shows undeserved favor (from chen, "grace"). Here it is the reason God hears the poor man: not because he has a legal claim, but because God is that kind of God. In 34:6 the LORD proclaims himself "compassionate and kind" (rachum vechannun), a formula repeated through the Bible (Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2).
orig: חַנּוּן אָנִי (channun ani), "I am gracious"

a: Do not treat God with contempt
p: Elohim here may be God, the judges, or (in the Greek) "gods." Paul quotes the second half in Acts.
b: The first half can be read three ways. (1) "Do not curse God": blasphemy, as in Leviticus 24:15–16. (2) "Do not curse the judges": Targum Onqelos and Rashi, matching "a leader of your people" in the second half. (3) "Do not revile the gods": the Greek Septuagint has the plural theous, and Philo (Life of Moses 2.205) and Josephus (Against Apion 2.237; Antiquities 4.207) say Jews were forbidden to insult other nations' gods, out of respect for the name "God." In Acts 23:5 Paul, rebuked for insulting the high priest, quotes the second half: "you will not speak badly of a ruler of your people." The KJV follows the Greek sense in the first half: "Thou shalt not revile the gods."
orig: אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל (Elohim lo teqallel), "God / judges you shall not curse"

a: from your full harvest and from your dripping presses
p: The Hebrew is poetic: "your fullness and your tear," meaning grain and the juice of grapes and olives.
b: Mele'atekha, "your fullness," is the ripe grain; dim'akha, from the word for "tear" (dim'ah), is the liquid that drips from wine and olive presses. Both are first fruits owed to God, and the command is not to be slow to bring them. Numbers 18:12–13 and Deuteronomy 18:4 give the first grain, wine and oil to the priests.
orig: מְלֵאָתְךָ וְדִמְעֲךָ (mele'atekha vedim'akha), "your fullness and your tear"

a: Give me the firstborn of your sons.
p: Firstborn sons were bought back, not sacrificed. Some scholars think the law rejects child sacrifice.
b: Exodus 13:2, 13–15 and 34:20 explain that firstborn sons are "redeemed" with a payment, five shekels in Numbers 18:15–16, and Jewish families still hold the ceremony of pidyon haben, "redemption of the son." Luke 2:22–24 tells how Mary and Joseph presented Jesus at the temple to fulfill this law. Some scholars, such as Jon Levenson, argue that verses like this one, which do not mention redemption, preserve a memory of a time when the idea of sacrificing a firstborn was thinkable, and that the Bible's story, from the binding of Isaac to the Passover, transforms it; Ezekiel 20:25–26 is a puzzling text in that discussion. Most readers take this verse as shorthand for the fuller law.

a: on the eighth day give it to me
p: A newborn animal stays with its mother seven days, like a boy's circumcision on the eighth day.
b: Leviticus 22:27 repeats the rule for all sacrificial animals: seven days with the mother, offered from the eighth on. The pattern matches circumcision on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). Readers have seen compassion in it, like the laws against slaughtering a mother and her young on the same day (Leviticus 22:28) and taking a mother bird with her eggs (Deuteronomy 22:6–7). Others see a ritual idea: a creature must live through one full week, a complete cycle of creation, before it belongs to God.

a: throw it to the dogs.
p: The Yiddish word "treif," non-kosher food, comes from terefah, "torn," in this verse.
b: Terefah means an animal torn by a predator. Because it died without being properly slaughtered and drained of blood, Israel may not eat it (Leviticus 17:15; Leviticus 22:8; Ezekiel 44:31). In rabbinic law terefah came to cover any animal with a fatal defect, and in Yiddish treif became the general word for food that is not kosher. Why the dogs? The Mekhilta answers that God rewards every creature: the dogs did not bark on the night Israel left Egypt (11:7), so they receive this meat. Holiness here touches the dinner table: a holy people eats differently.
orig: טְרֵפָה (terefah), "torn"

a: Do not pass along a false rumor.
p: The rabbis read this verse as a ban on spreading or even accepting slander, and on hearing one side in court.
b: Lo tissa shema shav can mean "do not raise" or "do not accept" a false report. The Talmud read it both ways: it forbids telling slander (lashon hara) and listening to it (Pesachim 118a), and it forbids a judge to hear one party when the other is not present (Sanhedrin 7b). The verse begins a short unit on justice in court (23:1–9), framed by warnings about false testimony and about the foreigner. "A witness for violence" (ed chamas) is one whose testimony helps the guilty harm the innocent, like the false witnesses against Naboth (1 Kings 21:10–13).
orig: לֹא תִשָּׂא שֵׁמַע שָׁוְא (lo tissa shema shav)

a: Do not follow the many into evil.
p: The rabbis read the end of this verse in reverse, as a rule to decide by majority vote.
b: The plain sense warns against going along with the many. But the last words, acharei rabbim lehattot, "after the many, to turn aside," were read by the rabbis on their own as a positive rule: "incline after the majority." This became the basis of majority decision in Jewish courts (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6; Bava Metzia 59b). In the famous story of the oven of Akhnai, Rabbi Eliezer calls on miracles and even a voice from heaven to support his view, and Rabbi Joshua answers, "It is not in heaven" (Deuteronomy 30:12, KJV): the law follows the majority of the sages. The verse thus holds both a warning against mob pressure and a charter for collective decision.
orig: אַחֲרֵי רַבִּים לְהַטֹּת (acharei rabbim lehattot)

a: And do not tip the scales for a poor man in his case.
t: Even the poor get no special treatment
p: Justice must be blind both ways. Some scholars suggest an old copying error; Leviticus 19:15 supports the text.
b: It seems odd for a law full of care for the poor to warn against favoring them, so some scholars have proposed reading gadol, "a great man," instead of dal, "a poor man" (the two words differ by one letter in Hebrew script). But Leviticus 19:15 says both: do not favor the poor or honor the great; judge your neighbor fairly. Deuteronomy 1:17 adds: hear small and great alike. Rashi explains that a judge must not say, "He is poor, and the rich man is obliged to support him; I will rule in his favor so that he gets support with dignity." Mercy belongs outside the court, not in the verdict.
orig: וְדָל לֹא תֶהְדַּר בְּרִיבוֹ (vedal lo tehdar berivo)

a: If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey straying
p: Even an enemy's animal must be returned. Proverbs and Jesus take the idea further.
b: Deuteronomy 22:1–4 gives the same law about "your brother's" ox; this version says "your enemy" and "someone who hates you" (23:5). Proverbs 25:21–22, quoted by Paul in Romans 12:20, tells us to feed a hungry enemy. Jesus' command to love your enemies (Matthew 5:43–48) builds on this tradition; the words "hate your enemy" that he quotes are found nowhere in the Torah. The rabbis noted that the law first concerns the suffering of the animal (tsa'ar ba'alei chayyim, Bava Metzia 32b) and then the healing of a quarrel: helping your enemy's donkey can end the enmity.
r: Deuteronomy 22:1–4; Proverbs 24:17; Proverbs 25:21–22; Matthew 5:43–48; Luke 6:27; Romans 12:20

a: You must work it loose together with him
p: The verb azav usually means "leave," but here it must mean "help." A related word may explain it.
b: The Hebrew plays on one verb three times: "refrain from azov to him, azov ta'azov with him." Azav normally means "abandon," which gives nonsense here. Some scholars (Umberto Cassuto and others) connect it with a second root found in Ugaritic and South Arabian meaning "arrange, set in order, help," which also appears in Nehemiah 3:8. The sense is then: when you would rather walk away, you must unload it together with him. Deuteronomy 22:4 says the same with a clearer verb: "Be sure to help him get it back on its feet." Its Hebrew, haqem taqim immo, is literally "you must surely raise it with him."
orig: עָזֹב תַּעֲזֹב עִמּוֹ (azov ta'azov immo)

a: for I will not count the wicked as righteous
p: If a human court frees the guilty, God's court will not. The Greek adds "for bribes."
b: The verse ends by moving from the human court to God's: even if a guilty man escapes through a false charge, God will not "justify" (atsdiq) the wicked. Proverbs 17:15 calls both acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent "an abomination to the LORD." Paul's claim that God "justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5) deliberately echoes and turns this language, explaining that God does so through faith and the death of Christ, not by bribery or by pretending. The Greek Septuagint reads, "and you shall not acquit the ungodly for gifts," which ties the verse to the bribe in 23:8.
orig: לֹא־אַצְדִּיק רָשָׁע (lo-atsdiq rasha), "I will not declare the wicked righteous"

a: a bribe blinds those who see clearly
p: This proverb-like line returns in Deuteronomy and the prophets. Samuel's sons failed exactly here.
b: Deuteronomy 16:19 repeats it: "a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and turns the words of the righteous upside down." Samuel's sons "took bribes and twisted justice," and Israel asked for a king (1 Samuel 8:3–5). Isaiah 1:23 and Micah 3:11 condemn leaders who love bribes. The Talmud says that even a small favor can bend a judge, and tells of judges who refused to hear the case of a man who had helped them across a river or brushed a feather off their coat (Ketubot 105b). "Honest people" translates tsaddiqim, the righteous: even good judges are not immune.
r: Deuteronomy 16:19; 1 Samuel 8:3; 1 Samuel 12:3; Proverbs 15:27; Proverbs 17:23; Isaiah 1:23; Isaiah 5:23; Micah 3:11

a: You know the life of a foreigner from the inside
t: "You know the soul of the foreigner"
p: The Hebrew says Israel knows the nefesh, the inner life or feelings, of an outsider.
b: Nefesh means breath, life, self, desire. To know someone's nefesh is to know what it feels like to be him. The law repeats 22:21 almost word for word but adds this line, which turns memory into empathy. It is one of the clearest places where the Torah grounds an ethical rule not in a command alone but in shared experience. See the note at 22:21 and the topic on foreigners.
orig: אֶת־נֶפֶשׁ הַגֵּר (et-nefesh hagger), "the soul of the foreigner"

a: but in the seventh year let it go and leave it alone
p: Every seventh year the land rested and the poor could eat freely. The law is still observed in Israel.
b: Here the seventh-year rule is about the poor and the animals; Leviticus 25:1–7 calls it a Sabbath for the land itself, and Deuteronomy 15:1–11 adds a release of debts. Jews kept the Sabbath year in the Second Temple period: 1 Maccabees 6:49, 53 describes a food shortage during one, and Josephus says Julius Caesar excused the Jews from taxes in that year (Antiquities 14.202). When the release of debts made lenders refuse to lend, Hillel created the prozbul, a court document that kept loans collectable (Mishnah Sheviit 10:3). In the modern State of Israel, farmers either let fields rest every seventh year or use a legal sale of the land (the heter mechirah).
orig: תִּשְׁמְטֶנָּה וּנְטַשְׁתָּהּ (tishmetennah unetashtah), "you shall release it and leave it"

a: can catch their breath
p: The verb comes from nefesh, "breath." Exodus uses it for God himself after creation (31:17).
b: Yinnafesh, "he may catch his breath," comes from the same root as nefesh (see 23:9). The only other use of the verb in the Torah is for God at the end of creation (31:17), and the only other in the Bible is for David's tired men (2 Samuel 16:14). The slave woman's son and the foreigner get the same rest God took. This version of the Sabbath command, inside the Covenant Code, is entirely about the workers and the animals, not worship.
orig: וְיִנָּפֵשׁ (veyinnafesh), "and may catch his breath"

a: Do not even mention the names of other gods
p: Israel was not to invoke other gods' names in oaths or prayers. Hosea hopes the names of the Baals will be forgotten.
b: Hizkir, "call to mind, invoke," refers to using a god's name in an oath, a blessing or prayer. Joshua 23:7 repeats the command, and Psalm 16:4 says, "I will not pour drink offerings of blood to them, nor will I speak their names." Hosea 2:17 promises a day when God will remove the names of the Baals from Israel's mouth. The rabbis said one should not even say to a friend, "Wait for me beside such-and-such idol" (Sanhedrin 63b). Yet Israelite names often contained the name Baal (Jerubbaal, Eshbaal), which later scribes sometimes changed to boshet, "shame" (Ishbosheth in 2 Samuel 2:8).
r: Joshua 23:7; Psalm 16:4; Hosea 2:16–17; Zechariah 13:2; 2 Samuel 2:8; 1 Chronicles 8:33

a: Three times a year hold a feast for me.
p: "Three times" here is "three feet": the three festivals when Israelites walked to the sanctuary.
b: The Hebrew says shalosh regalim, "three feet," a rare way to say "three times," and Jewish tradition still calls Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot the Shalosh Regalim, the three foot-festivals or pilgrimage feasts. The verb chagag, "hold a feast," and the noun chag are related to the Arabic hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and probably first meant a procession or a sacred dance. The festivals are tied to the farming year (23:15–16).
orig: שָׁלֹשׁ רְגָלִים תָּחֹג (shalosh regalim tachog), "three feet you shall feast"

a: No one is to appear before my face with empty hands.
p: The Hebrew letters may first have said "see my face." The scribes' vowels say "appear before me."
b: The consonants of yera'u panai could be read yir'u panai, "they shall see my face," which many scholars think was the original idiom for visiting a sanctuary (compare Psalm 42:2, "When will I come / and appear before the face of God?", whose letters could also be read "see the face of God"). The Masoretic vowels make the verb passive, "they shall be seen before me," that is, "appear before me," probably to avoid saying that people see God's face (33:20). Both senses carry the point: a pilgrim comes into God's presence with a gift. The Plain English follows the Masoretic vowels; the variant shows the other reading.
orig: לֹא־יֵרָאוּ פָנַי רֵיקָם (lo-yera'u fanai reqam)

a: Keep also the Feast of Harvest
p: The three feasts follow the farm year: barley in spring, wheat in early summer, fruit and olives in autumn.
b: Unleavened Bread falls at the barley harvest in the month of Abib, "fresh ears," and is tied to the exodus (13:3–10). The Feast of Harvest comes at the end of the wheat harvest, seven weeks later, and is called the Feast of Weeks in 34:22 (Shavuot; in Greek, Pentecost). The Feast of Ingathering, later called Booths (Sukkot), comes "as the year goes out," in the autumn, when grapes and olives are gathered. The Gezer Calendar, a schoolboy's tablet from about 950 BC, lists the farming months beginning with "two months of ingathering," which shows an autumn new year like the one assumed here.

a: every male among you is to appear
p: The duty fell on men, but women and children came too. Jesus went up for the festivals.
b: The law obliges men, but women often made the journey: Hannah went to Shiloh every year (1 Samuel 1:3–7), and Deuteronomy 16:11, 14 includes sons, daughters, slaves, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows in the rejoicing. Luke 2:41–42 says Jesus' parents went to Jerusalem every year for Passover. In John's Gospel Jesus' ministry follows the pilgrim feasts (John 2:13; John 5:1; John 7:2, 10; John 12:12). The title "the Lord, the LORD" (ha'adon YHWH) presents God as master of the land whose produce the pilgrims bring.

a: The fat of my feast must not be left until morning.
p: The rabbis took "my sacrifice" here as the Passover lamb. Exodus 34:25 says so directly.
b: The parallel law in 34:25 names "the sacrifice of the Passover feast." So the rabbis read this verse as Passover rules: no leaven may be in one's house when the lamb is slaughtered (12:15–20), and nothing of it may be left until morning (12:10). The Masoretic Text says "my feast," as if God himself hosts the meal.

a: Do not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother.
p: This short law, repeated three times in the Torah, is the root of the Jewish separation of meat and dairy.
b: The rule appears here, in 34:26 and in Deuteronomy 14:21, and no one knows its first reason. The chapter page sets out the main explanations: a ban on a pagan rite (Maimonides), a law of compassion (Philo), and the rabbis' reading of the three times as three bans (Chullin 115b), the root of the Jewish separation of meat and dairy. The Ugaritic text once cited for a pagan rite (KTU 1.23) is now read very differently (Ratner and Zuckerman, 1986). Christians generally treat it as part of the food laws that Mark 7:19 and Acts 10 set aside.
orig: לֹא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ (lo-tevashel gedi bachalev immo)

a: I am sending an angel in front of you
p: A messenger who carries God's name: an angel, God's own presence, or (for many Christians) the Son of God?
b: This angel guards, leads and can refuse to forgive, and God's "name is in him" (23:21). Readers have given four main answers. (1) A created angel; the Talmud links him to Metatron, "whose name is like his Master's" (Sanhedrin 38b). (2) God's own presence, the "angel of the LORD" who speaks as God (3:2–6; Genesis 16:7–13); Ramban argued for this, comparing 33:14–15, where God's "presence" goes with them. (3) Many church fathers, beginning with Justin Martyr (Dialogue 75), saw the Son of God before his birth as Jesus, noting that the leader who brought Israel into the land was Joshua, whose name is Jesus in Greek. (4) Malachi 3:1 reuses this verse, and Mark 1:2 joins the two: "Look, I send my messenger before your face," applied to John the Baptist.
orig: הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי שֹׁלֵחַ מַלְאָךְ (hinneh anokhi sholeach mal'akh)
r: 3:2–6; 14:19; 32:34; 33:2, 14–15; Genesis 16:7–13; Joshua 5:13–15; Malachi 3:1; Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27; 1 Corinthians 10:4

a: my name is in him
p: To have God's name is to carry his authority. Christians link it with the name given to Jesus.
b: In the Bible a name stands for a person's presence and authority. God puts his name on the place of worship (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11), on Israel (Numbers 6:27) and here on his messenger. The angel acts with God's own authority, so rebellion against him is rebellion against God. New Testament writers say God gave Jesus "the name above every name" (Philippians 2:9–11) and that Jesus kept his disciples "in your name, the name you have given me" (John 17:11–12). Jewish mystical traditions developed the idea of an angel bearing the divine name.
orig: כִּי שְׁמִי בְּקִרְבּוֹ (ki shemi beqirbo), "for my name is within him"
r: Numbers 6:27; Deuteronomy 12:5, 11; 1 Kings 8:29; Philippians 2:9–11; John 17:11–12; Revelation 19:12–13

a: the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites
p: Lists of Canaan's peoples vary between six and seven names. Some were real peoples; others are obscure.
b: Similar lists appear often (3:8, 17; 33:2; 34:11; Deuteronomy 7:1). Deuteronomy 7:1 has seven, adding the Girgashites, and the Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint often add them where the Hebrew has six. The Canaanites and Amorites are well known from ancient records ("Amurru" in Mesopotamian texts). The "Hittites" here are probably not the empire of Asia Minor but local groups with that name. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David (2 Samuel 5:6–9). The Perizzites and Hivites are known only from the Bible; "Perizzite" may mean village-dwellers.

a: smash their standing stones to bits
p: Canaanite standing stones must be smashed, yet Moses sets up twelve of his own in the next chapter.
b: A matsevah is an upright stone set up as a memorial or a sign of a god's presence. Jacob set one up at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), and Moses sets up twelve at Sinai (24:4), but Canaanite stones linked to other gods are to be broken (34:13), and Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids Israel to set up any. Archaeologists have found standing stones at many sites, including the Israelite shrine at Arad and the large stones at Gezer. Many scholars see a development from acceptance to rejection; others say the difference was always in what a stone stood for.
orig: וְשַׁבֵּר תְּשַׁבֵּר מַצֵּבֹתֵיהֶם (veshabber teshabber matsevotehem)
r: 24:4; 34:13; Genesis 28:18; Genesis 31:45; Leviticus 26:1; Deuteronomy 7:5; Deuteronomy 12:3; Deuteronomy 16:22

a: I will send the hornet in front of you
p: Tsir'ah may be a real hornet, a picture of panic, a plague, or (one theory) the armies of Egypt.
b: Tsir'ah appears only here, in Deuteronomy 7:20 and in Joshua 24:12, which says the hornet drove out two Amorite kings, "not by your sword or your bow." The Septuagint and Wisdom 12:8–9 say "wasps." Many scholars take it as a picture of the terror of 23:27 or of a plague. John Garstang (1931) suggested it stood for Egyptian armies that weakened Canaan, since the bee was a symbol of the pharaoh's rule over Lower Egypt; few hold that view now. The point is that God, not Israel, wins the land.
orig: הַצִּרְעָה (hatsir'ah), "the hornet"

a: I will not drive them all out in one year
p: God promises a gradual takeover. The book of Judges and archaeology both show a long, slow process.
b: Deuteronomy 7:22 repeats the reason: if the land emptied too fast, wild animals would take over. Judges 2:20–3:4 gives other reasons the nations remained: to test Israel and to teach the next generation war. Many archaeologists, such as Israel Finkelstein and William Dever, see Israel emerging gradually in the central hill country around 1200 BC, largely from people already in Canaan; others, such as Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier, defend an entry from outside with limited destruction. The command to drive out and destroy the peoples (23:23, 31–33) is among the hardest in Scripture for modern readers; see the topic on the promised land.

a: from the Sea of Reeds to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River
p: From the Gulf of Aqaba to the Mediterranean, and from the desert to the Euphrates. Reached only under Solomon, if then.
b: Yam Suf, "the Sea of Reeds," often called "the Red Sea," here seems to mean the Gulf of Aqaba, where Solomon's port of Ezion-geber lay "on the shore of the Sea of Reeds" (1 Kings 9:26); on the name and the sea of the crossing, see 13:18 and 15:4. "The Sea of the Philistines" is the Mediterranean, "the wilderness" the southern desert, and "the River" the Euphrates. The promise matches the one to Abram; in this site's Plain English, Genesis 15:18 reads: "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates." Only Solomon's rule is said to reach so far (1 Kings 4:21, 24), and many historians doubt even that. Most readers take the borders as an ideal of God's promise.
orig: מִיַּם־סוּף (miyyam-suf), "from the Sea of Reeds"
r: Genesis 15:18–21; Deuteronomy 1:7; Deuteronomy 11:24; Joshua 1:4; 1 Kings 4:21, 24; 1 Kings 9:26

a: that would be a trap for you
p: Living side by side with Canaanite worship would lure Israel away. Judges says it did.
b: Moqesh is a bird trap or snare. Judges 2:3 has the angel of the LORD announce the result: "their gods will become a trap for you." Psalm 106:34–36 says Israel did not destroy the peoples but mingled with them, learned their ways and served their idols, "and these became a trap for them." The same word appears in Joshua 23:13. Christian readers often apply the warning spiritually, to what draws the heart from God (2 Corinthians 6:14–7:1; 1 John 5:21).
orig: לְמוֹקֵשׁ (lemoqesh), "for a snare"

a: Nadab and Abihu
p: Nadab and Abihu see God here and die later for offering "strange fire." The rabbis linked the two scenes.
b: Nadab and Abihu are Aaron's two oldest sons (6:23). In Leviticus 10:1–2 they offer "unauthorized fire" before the LORD and are consumed by fire from his presence. The rabbis connected their death to this chapter: Rashi on 24:10–11 says they looked at God with too much boldness while eating and drinking and deserved death then, but God did not want to spoil the joy of the covenant day and waited (compare Leviticus Rabbah 20:10). The text of Exodus itself says only that God did not harm them (24:11).

a: seventy of the elders of Israel
p: Seventy recalls the seventy nations of Genesis 10 and the seventy who went down to Egypt.
b: Seventy is a round number of fullness: the seventy descendants of Jacob who went to Egypt (1:5), the seventy nations of Genesis 10, the seventy elders who receive a share of Moses' spirit (Numbers 11:16–25). The later Jewish high court, the Sanhedrin, had seventy-one members, modeled on Moses and the seventy (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6). Jesus sends out seventy (or seventy-two) disciples in Luke 10:1, perhaps with this background in view. The elders represent the whole people at the covenant meal.
orig: וְשִׁבְעִים מִזִּקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (veshiv'im mizziqnei Yisra'el)

a: All the people answered with a single voice
p: The people agree before (19:8) and after (24:3, 7) they hear the laws. Joshua later repeats the scene.
b: The people's "we will do" comes three times (19:8; 24:3; 24:7), each time after hearing more. The ceremony of chapter 24 has the shape of a treaty: the terms are read, the people agree, the agreement is written down, witnesses (the twelve stones) are set up, and the covenant is sealed with sacrifice and a meal. Joshua 24:16–27 renews the covenant in the same way at Shechem, with a stone as witness, and 2 Kings 23:1–3 tells how Josiah read "every word of the covenant scroll" to the people, who took their stand on it. Nehemiah 8–10 has Ezra read the law and the people sign a pledge.

a: Moses wrote all the LORD's words
t: The first book of the Bible?
p: Moses writes the "words" and "rulings," and the result is called "the scroll of the covenant."
b: The "scroll of the covenant" read in 24:7 is, by the plain sense of the story, a written copy of what God has just spoken, 20:22–23:33 (and perhaps the Ten Words). That is why scholars call that section the Covenant Code or Book of the Covenant. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see here the beginning of Moses' writing of the Torah. The rabbis debated whether the scroll held Genesis to this point as well (Rashi on 24:4, 7, following the Mekhilta). Critical scholars generally see the Covenant Code as one of the oldest law collections in the Pentateuch, though dated anywhere from the time of the judges to the 700s BC.

a: twelve standing stones for the twelve tribes of Israel
p: The twelve stones stand for the tribes as witnesses to the covenant. Joshua and Elijah set up twelve stones too.
b: Jacob set up a single standing stone at Bethel; in this site's Plain English, Genesis 28:18 says he took the stone he had slept on and "set it up as a standing stone." Moses sets up twelve, one per tribe, at the foot of the mountain. They may serve as witnesses, as the stone of Joshua 24:26–27 "heard everything the LORD said." Joshua sets up twelve stones from the Jordan (Joshua 4:1–9), and Elijah builds his altar on Carmel with twelve stones (1 Kings 18:31). The high priest's breastpiece carries twelve stones with the tribes' names (28:21), and Revelation's new Jerusalem has twelve gates and twelve foundations (Revelation 21:12–14).
r: 28:21; Genesis 28:18; Genesis 31:45–52; Joshua 4:1–9; Joshua 24:26–27; 1 Kings 18:31; Revelation 21:12–14

a: He sent young men from the Israelites
p: No priests are ordained yet. Targum Onqelos and Rashi say these "young men" were the firstborn.
b: The sacrifices are offered by na'arei benei Yisra'el, "young men of the Israelites." Targum Onqelos renders "the firstborn of the Israelites," and Rashi agrees, following the tradition that firstborn sons served as priests until the Levites took their place (Numbers 3:11–13; see Exodus 19:22). Others think young men were chosen simply for strength, since handling bulls is hard work. Moses himself handles the blood, acting as priest.
orig: נַעֲרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (na'arei benei Yisra'el)

a: half of the blood he dashed on the altar
p: Half the blood goes on the altar, which stands for God, and half on the people. One life now binds both.
b: Blood is life (Leviticus 17:11), and splitting it between the altar and the people joins the two parties in one bond. No exact parallel is known, but ancient treaties were often sealed with a sacrifice. Texts from Mari (1700s BC) speak of "killing a donkey foal" to make a covenant, and an Aramaic treaty from Sefire (700s BC) curses the oath-breaker: as this calf is cut in two, so may he be cut. Compare the split animals of Genesis 15:9–18 and Jeremiah 34:18–19. The verb zaraq means to toss or dash liquid from a bowl, not to sprinkle a few drops.
orig: זָרַק עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (zaraq al-hammizbeach), "he dashed on the altar"

a: we will do, and we will listen
t: Na'aseh venishma: "We will do, and we will hear"
p: The rabbis praised Israel for promising to do before they had heard, as angels do.
b: Na'aseh venishma literally means "we will do and we will hear" (or "obey"). The Talmud tells that when Israel put "we will do" before "we will hear," 600,000 angels came and set two crowns on every Israelite, one for each word, and a heavenly voice asked, "Who revealed to my children this secret that the angels use?" quoting Psalm 103:20, which describes angels who "do his word, listening to the voice of his word" (Shabbat 88a). The phrase became a byword for commitment before full understanding. Others note that "hear" (shama) often means "obey" in Hebrew, so the pair may simply mean "we will obey completely."
orig: נַעֲשֶׂה וְנִשְׁמָע (na'aseh venishma)

a: Here is the blood of the covenant
t: "The blood of the covenant" and the Last Supper
p: Jesus takes up these words at the Last Supper: "This is my blood of the covenant."
b: At the Last Supper Jesus takes the cup and says, "This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many" (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28 adds "so that sins can be forgiven"); Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 call it "the new covenant in my blood," echoing Jeremiah 31:31. Hebrews 9:18–22 retells this scene, adding details not in Exodus: water, scarlet wool, hyssop, and the sprinkling of the scroll itself. Zechariah 9:11 speaks of prisoners set free "because of the blood of your covenant." Jewish readers point to the Sinai covenant as permanent and still in force (Leviticus 26:44–45; Psalm 105:8–10); Christians read the new covenant as its fulfillment, and they debate whether it renews or replaces the old one.
orig: הִנֵּה דַם־הַבְּרִית (hinneh dam-habberit), "here is the blood of the covenant"
r: Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Hebrews 9:18–22; Hebrews 10:29; Hebrews 13:20; Zechariah 9:11; 1 Peter 1:2; Jeremiah 31:31–34

a: that the LORD has cut with you
p: Hebrew says one "cuts" a covenant, probably from the old rite of cutting animals in two.
b: The usual Hebrew idiom is karat berit, "cut a covenant." It probably comes from rites like the one in Genesis 15, where animals are cut in half and God's presence passes between the pieces; in this site's Plain English, Genesis 15:18 reads: "On that day the LORD cut a covenant with Abram." Jeremiah 34:18–19 describes the leaders of Judah walking between the halves of a calf and so calling down its fate on themselves if they broke their word. Here the blood replaces the cut pieces as the sign of the bond.
orig: אֲשֶׁר כָּרַת יְהוָה עִמָּכֶם (asher karat YHWH immakhem)

a: They saw the God of Israel.
p: Elsewhere no one can see God and live. How did they see him? Ancient readers already softened the verse.
b: God tells Moses "no human being can see me and stay alive" (33:20), and John 1:18 says "nobody has ever seen God." Yet here seventy-four people see him. Ancient translations soften it: the Septuagint says "they saw the place where the God of Israel stood" (see the variant), and Targum Onqelos says "they saw the glory of the God of Israel." Maimonides read "seeing" as understanding with the mind (Guide 1.4–5). Justin Martyr and many early Christian writers after him said that whenever God was seen in the Old Testament it was the Son, who makes the Father known. Many critical scholars think the verse preserves an old, bold tradition. Notice that the text describes only what was under his feet.
orig: וַיִּרְאוּ אֵת אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (vayyir'u et Elohei Yisra'el)
r: 33:18–23; Numbers 12:8; Isaiah 6:1–5; Ezekiel 1:26–28; John 1:18; John 14:9; 1 Timothy 6:16

a: Under his feet was what looked like a floor of blue lapis stone, as pure as the sky itself.
p: The Hebrew sappir was probably lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone that ancient art used for the sky.
b: Sappir gives English "sapphire," but ancient writers describe it as blue with gold flecks, which fits lapis lazuli, prized in Egypt and Mesopotamia and used to picture the heavens. Ezekiel sees God's throne "like sappir" above the dome of heaven (Ezekiel 1:26; Ezekiel 10:1). Ke'etsem hashamayim, "like the very bone of the heavens," means the substance of the sky itself. Rashi notes the word livnat, "pavement" or "brickwork": a brick lay before God throughout Israel's slavery, as a sign that he shared their suffering in the brick pits of Egypt (Rashi, from the midrash). The vision under God's feet becomes the floor of the throne room in Revelation 4:6, "a sea of glass, clear as crystal."
orig: כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר וּכְעֶצֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם לָטֹהַר (kema'aseh livnat hassappir ukhe'etsem hashamayim latohar)

a: They looked upon God, and they ate and drank.
p: The covenant ends with a meal in God's presence. Jews and Christians read it as a picture of the age to come.
b: Eating together sealed agreements in the ancient world (Genesis 26:30; Genesis 31:54). Here the leaders of Israel eat in God's presence and live. The Talmud uses this verse for the world to come: there is no eating or drinking there, but the righteous sit with crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of God's presence, as it says, "they looked upon God, and they ate and drank" (Berakhot 17a), that is, the vision itself was their food. Other rabbis read the meal less kindly (see 24:1). Christian readers see the Lord's Supper and the promised banquet of the kingdom: Isaiah 25:6–8 places a feast for all peoples "on this mountain," and Jesus speaks of many who will eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11; Revelation 19:9).
orig: וַיֶּחֱזוּ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים וַיֹּאכְלוּ וַיִּשְׁתּוּ (vayyechezu et-ha'Elohim vayyokhelu vayyishtu)
r: 18:12; Genesis 31:54; Isaiah 25:6–8; Matthew 8:11; Matthew 26:29; Luke 22:15–20; Revelation 19:9

a: I will give you the stone tablets, with the law and the command
t: Tablets, Torah and the oral tradition
p: The Talmud read each phrase of this verse as a different part of Scripture and of the Oral Torah.
b: Rabbi Levi bar Hama read the verse word by word: "the stone tablets" are the Ten Words; "the law" (torah) is the Pentateuch; "the command" (mitsvah) is the Mishnah; "that I have written" is the Prophets and the Writings; "to instruct them" is the Talmud: all of it was given to Moses at Sinai (Berakhot 5a). This is a classic statement of the belief that the Oral Torah, the tradition of interpretation, goes back to Sinai along with the written text (compare Avot 1:1). Christian readers have often contrasted the stone tablets with the law written "on tablets of human hearts" (2 Corinthians 3:3; Jeremiah 31:33).
orig: אֶת־לֻחֹת הָאֶבֶן וְהַתּוֹרָה וְהַמִּצְוָה (et-luchot ha'even vehattorah vehammitsvah)

a: together with Joshua his helper
p: Joshua goes partway up the mountain with Moses. He is being trained to succeed him.
b: Mesharet, "helper, attendant," describes someone who serves a leader and learns from him, as Elisha served Elijah (1 Kings 19:21). Joshua appears at the battle with Amalek (17:9–14), climbs partway with Moses here, meets him coming down and mistakes the noise of the golden calf for war (32:17), and stays in the tent of meeting when Moses leaves it (33:11). The rabbis taught that Moses received the Torah at Sinai and passed it to Joshua (Avot 1:1), the beginning of the chain of tradition.
orig: וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ מְשָׁרְתוֹ (viYhoshua mesharto), "and Joshua his attendant"

a: Look, Aaron and Hur are with you.
p: Hur held up Moses' hands in 17:12. Jewish tradition says he died resisting the golden calf.
b: In the story, Hur appears only in 17:10–12 and here; the lists at 31:2, 35:30 and 38:22 name him as the grandfather of Bezalel, the tabernacle's master craftsman (also 1 Chronicles 2:19–20). Josephus calls him the husband of Miriam (Antiquities 3.54), while the rabbis call him her son (Sotah 11b). Hur vanishes from the story before the golden calf, and the Talmud explains why: when he rebuked the people for making the calf, they killed him, and Aaron, seeing this, gave in out of fear (Sanhedrin 7a). Aaron, left in charge here, will fail that test in chapter 32.

a: The glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai
p: The verb shakhan, "dwell, settle," gives the later Jewish word for God's presence, the Shekhinah.
b: Vayyishkon, "and it settled," comes from shakhan, the root of mishkan (25:9), "dwelling, tabernacle," and of the rabbinic word Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence among his people. What rests on the mountain here will move into the tabernacle at the end of the book (40:34–35), and the mountain becomes portable. John 1:14 uses a Greek verb that sounds like the Hebrew: the Word "tented" (eskēnōsen) among us, and we saw his glory.
orig: וַיִּשְׁכֹּן כְּבוֹד־יְהוָה (vayyishkon kevod-YHWH), "and the glory of the LORD settled"

a: the cloud covered it six days. On the seventh day he called to Moses
p: The pattern of creation returns: six days of waiting, a call on the seventh. The Gospels' Transfiguration echoes it.
b: Moses waits six days in the cloud before God speaks, like the six days of creation before the seventh (Genesis 1:1–2:3). Many scholars note that the instructions for the tabernacle that follow (chapters 25–31) seem to build a small world for God to live in, ending with the Sabbath (31:12–17). The Gospels tell the Transfiguration "after six days": Jesus goes up a high mountain, his face shines, a cloud covers them and a voice speaks from it, and Moses appears with Elijah (Mark 9:2–8; Matthew 17:1–8). The rabbis said the six days were for Moses' purification before entering the cloud (Yoma 4a).

a: The LORD's glory looked like a fire that eats everything
p: From below, God's glory looked like fire. Deuteronomy and Hebrews call God a fire that eats.
b: Deuteronomy 4:24 says "the LORD your God is a devouring fire, a jealous God," and Deuteronomy 9:3 says he goes ahead of Israel as "a devouring fire." Both use the Hebrew of this verse, esh okhelet, a fire that eats. Hebrews 12:18–29 contrasts Sinai, with its fire, darkness and terror, with Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and yet ends: "our God is a fire that eats." The same fire that terrifies the crowd is the place Moses enters (24:18). Christians have often read this as law and gospel: God's holiness is not less at Zion than at Sinai, but there is now a way in.
orig: כְּאֵשׁ אֹכֶלֶת (ke'esh okhelet), "like a devouring fire"

a: Moses stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
p: Forty days on the mountain without food. Elijah and Jesus also fast forty days.
b: Deuteronomy 9:9 adds that Moses ate no bread and drank no water; he spends a second forty days after the golden calf (34:28; Deuteronomy 9:18; Deuteronomy 10:10). Elijah walks forty days to Horeb, the same mountain, on the strength of one meal (1 Kings 19:8), and Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness before his ministry (Matthew 4:2). Jewish tradition dates Moses' descent to the seventeenth of Tammuz, when he broke the tablets, a fast day that also mourns the breaching of Jerusalem's walls (Mishnah Taanit 4:6).
orig: אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לָיְלָה (arba'im yom ve'arba'im laylah)

a: slave
p: Older and some newer versions say "servant" here. This site says "slave," and the choice is part of a real debate.
b: Eved comes from avad, "work, serve," and covers a bought laborer, a king's official and a worshiper ("Moses the servant of the LORD"). The KJV and NIV say "servant" in this law; the ESV, NRSV and this site say "slave," because the person is bought (21:2), may be beaten (21:20) and is called "his money" (21:21). Paul Copan (Is God a Moral Monster?, 2011) and Walter Kaiser argue that the Hebrew debt-servant was closer to an indentured worker with legal rights than to chattel slavery. Hector Avalos (Slavery, Abolitionism, and the Ethics of Biblical Scholarship, 2011) replies that "servant" hides real ownership, and points to Leviticus 25:44–46, which lets Israelites hold foreigners as property for life. Rabbinic law separates the eved Ivri, a Hebrew bondman with strong rights, from the eved Kena'ani, a foreign slave (Kiddushin 14b–22b).
orig: עֶבֶד (eved)

a: got word of everything God had done for Moses and for Israel, his people
t: Claude's theory: two kinds of outsider
p: My own reading: chapters 17 and 18 set Amalek and Jethro side by side as two answers the nations give to Israel.
b: Claude's theory. Chapters 17 and 18 seem to be placed side by side on purpose. In both, outsiders come to Israel in the wilderness. Amalek comes to attack the weary (17:8; Deuteronomy 25:18); Jethro comes because he has heard what God did, and he blesses, sacrifices and eats with Israel's elders (18:1–12). Amalek's story ends with an altar and a war "one generation after another" (17:16); Jethro's ends with a shared meal before God and Israel's first courts. If the pairing is meant, it says the nations are not all one thing: some are enemies, some are teachers. When Saul later fights Amalek, he first warns the Kenites, Jethro's people, to leave (1 Samuel 15:6). Some medieval commentators noticed the contrast, but the reading here is mine.
